events.text: The first night of the Thousand Days. You sit on the grave mound under the full moon with your tails laid behind you like a folded fan, and say it out loud, because the old rules say it must be said out loud: a thousand days, and no harm to anyone. Not a hen. Not a breath. The moon does not answer. A dog in the village below barks twice and stops, as if someone had told it to.

choices.text: Say it again, slower, so the moon cannot pretend it did not hear

effects.log: You say it three times, each slower than the last. On the third the frost on the mound creaks under you like a floorboard. Day one. Nine hundred and ninety-nine to go, and the first of them begins at dawn.

choices.text: Count the days on a pine root with your claw, one scratch each dawn

effects.log: One scratch. The root is old and hard and will keep the count better than you will. You have heard of foxes who lost count at six hundred and started again out of honesty. You will not lose count.

choices.text: Go down and tell Banya, so someone else will know

effects.log: Your aunt pours you barley tea in her good jacket and listens without blinking. "Out loud?" she says. "Good. Everyone who tries it quietly fails. Come and tell me every hundredth day. I will pretend to be surprised."

events.text: Some way into the count. An old soldier who drinks at your table every market day stays after the others have gone, and leans across the counter, and says very quietly: "I was on the hill road the night of the frost. I saw you sit down on that mound. I counted your tails." He is drunk. He is also not wrong, and he is waiting to see what you will do about it.

choices.text: Pour him another cup and let him talk

effects.log: He talks until the lamp is low: about a war forty years ago, about a fox that once led his company out of a marsh in the dark, about how he has never told anyone, and will not now. When he goes, he leaves the coins on the counter and the secret in the cup.

choices.text: Walk him home through the rain under your own umbrella

effects.log: Halfway to his gate he says, "You could have made me forget." You could have. "I know," you say. He laughs all the way to his door, and in the morning he remembers everything, and comes to drink as usual, and never mentions it again.

choices.text: Lead him home by a road that takes all night

effects.log: Foxfire, three bends of the same lane, a ditch he steps into twice. By dawn he is sure he dreamed the whole thing, the hill and the tails and you. It is not harm. It is not kindness either, and the moon, you think, noticed the difference.

events.text: Deeper into the count. A child sleeps by your brazier all winter with a fever, brought in from the snow by a mother who could not pay the physician. The child's breath is warm across the room. You can smell it from the door: warm as new rice, quick as a sparrow's. The bead in your mouth turns over in its sleep like a dog dreaming of a hare.

choices.text: Open the window and sit by it all night, in the cold

effects.log: All winter the window is open and you sit in the draught with your back to the room. The fever breaks in the eleventh month on its own. The child never knows anything, except that the keeper of the house was always cold, and always kind. (-4 health)

choices.text: Lend the bead for one night, to break the fever

effects.log: The bead passes on your breath and you sit through the night counting the child's breaths instead of wanting them. At dawn the bead comes back warm and the fever is gone. Lending is not taking. The vow holds, and so do you.

choices.text: Send for the physician, and pay with the mask's savings

effects.log: The physician comes, grumbling, and stays three days, and the fever goes. You stand outside in the snow the whole time, which the physician thinks is very touching. It is the only place in the house you can stand.

events.text: Late in the count. At the winter market a fur-trader has a red pelt hung up on a pole with the others, and its two forepaws are white, as if it had stepped in snow. It could be White-Paw. It could be White-Paw's grandchild, or nobody you ever knew. The trader sees you looking and names a price. Not many days now, and the vow is kept.

choices.text: Buy it, and bury it on the mound where you were born

effects.log: You trade a whole season of the mask's work for it, and carry it up the hill under your coat, and dig with your hands. The trader thinks you are making a fur collar. You are making a grave. The count goes on, lighter by one.

choices.text: Walk past, and do not look at the paws again

effects.log: You walk past at the speed of somebody with an errand. Behind you the trader calls the price again, lower. You do not stop. It is the hardest hundred steps of the thousand days.

choices.text: Find out which hunter sold it, and make his night a long one

effects.log: You find him at a wine-house and wait. Foxfire on the marsh road, a lantern that goes the wrong way, and a fall in the dark that does not kill him. By morning he is lame, and the vow is broken near the end, and you knew it would be when you stood up.

events.text: The day after the thousandth day. The moon is up as it always is. You did not hurt anyone. You sit on the mound with the warm bead in your mouth and find you do not know what to do with yourself now that nothing is forbidden and nothing needs refusing. A thousand days of not, and now an ordinary morning.

choices.text: Go down and do one small kind thing nobody asked for

effects.log: You mend the gate of a widow's yard while she sleeps, and leave. A small thing. It is the first kindness in a thousand days that was not also a refusal, and it tastes different. Lighter.

choices.text: Sit until the next dawn and remember every temptation

effects.log: The drunk, the child, the pelt, the long nights. You go through them one by one, like beads on a string. None of them was easy. All of them are yours now, the way scars are.

choices.text: Tell someone of your mask a single true thing

effects.log: "I made a promise a long time ago," you tell them over the evening rice, "and today I finished keeping it." They do not ask what. They pour you more tea, and say they are proud of you, and do not know why they are crying.

events.text: The vow is broken. The scratches on the pine root stop partway along, and there is nothing to be done about the ones that are already there. The moon does not say anything; it does not need to. Heaven, the old foxes say, counts three broken vows and then stops counting.

choices.text: Swear it again at the very next full moon

effects.log: You scratch a line under the old count and start again beside it, at one. The root has room. Whether heaven has patience is another matter, and not one you can scratch into a pine.

choices.text: Wait a few years before trying again, until you trust yourself

effects.log: Not yet. You go about the hills for a while without promising anything to anyone. It is restful, and a little shameful, and you know you will go back to the mound in the end.

choices.text: Ask the moon out loud whether it is worth it

effects.log: The moon goes behind a cloud and comes out again. A shepherd on the next hill, who heard a voice from the graves asking the moon a question, never walks that road after dark again. That is all the answer you get.

events.text: The vow this time is counted against a life first. You know where the grave is: in the next village, a small mound with a stone that has the name cut shallow, because the family could not pay for deep. Every full moon of the vow you go and sit a little way off from it.

choices.text: Cut the grass on that grave every autumn before the family comes

effects.log: Every year, before Chuseok, the grave is already cut and the stone washed. The family thinks it is a cousin. The cousin thinks it is the family. Nobody thinks it is you, which is how it should be.

choices.text: Lend the bead to the family's sick grandchild

effects.log: A cough that will not go, in a house that has already buried one of its own because of you. The bead for a night. The cough goes. Nothing you give this house will ever balance it. You give it anyway.

choices.text: Tell the family what you are, and what you did

effects.log: The old man of the house hears it all, very still, and then goes out and comes back with a stick, and stands with it a long time, and puts it down. "Go," he says. "Do not come back." You go. You come back every year anyway, at night, to cut the grass.

events.text: A traveller asleep by your brazier, a strong young carter who drank too much and paid for a bed. Their breath fills the room like the smell of warm bread. The bead in your mouth aches with how dim it is. Nobody would know. Pale for a week, the carter would blame the drink.

choices.text: Go and sit outside until dawn

effects.log: You sit on the step with the frost coming up through your sandals. Inside, the carter snores. In the morning they pay, and thank you for the quiet, and go off whistling, exactly as pink as they came. (-3 health)

choices.text: Bow to the moon instead, from the yard

effects.log: A sliver of moon over the woodpile. You breathe it in, slowly, as if it were enough. It is not enough. It is what heaven counts, and you keep counting with it.

choices.text: Draw the thread, just this once

effects.log: You sit beside the carter while the lamp gutters and draw a thread of breath. The bead brightens like a coal. In the morning they are pale and blame the drink. You know better, and so, somewhere, does the moon.

events.text: A drunk in the market spits at your mask's feet and calls you a name that is almost right. A crowd gathers to see what the keeper will do. He falls asleep against your wall at sundown, mouth open, breathing like a bellows.

choices.text: Throw a blanket over him and leave him there

effects.log: In the morning he wakes under your blanket and has no idea whose it is. He brings it back three days later, folded, and does not say anything. Neither do you. The crowd, who wanted a fight, is disappointed.

choices.text: Answer him in the morning with a proverb he will remember

effects.log: "A dog that barks at the moon," you tell him, "loses its voice, not the moon." The market laughs. He goes red, then laughs too. By the end of the year he is drinking at your table like everyone else.

choices.text: Take a thread of his breath while he sleeps it off

effects.log: He is pale for a month and tells everyone the fox keeper cursed him. He is right, which makes it worse. The vow breaks with a sound only you hear, like a thread snapping in an empty room.

events.text: A hunter swaggers through the market in a cap of red fox, the brush hanging down behind like a plume. The fur is Ember's colour exactly: the red of a fire just before it goes. He tells everyone who will listen how he took it: a vixen at a rich man's henhouse, a trap baited with a chicken. He sleeps tonight at the inn on the hill road.

choices.text: Let him go home with his cap

effects.log: He goes home with it. You go home without anything, and sit on the mound and say Ember's name to the moon three times, which is all you have. It is not enough. It is not harm, either.

choices.text: Follow him to the inn, and only watch

effects.log: All night under the eaves of the inn, close enough to hear him breathe. Twice you get up. Twice you sit down again. At dawn he goes on his way, and so, eventually, do you.

choices.text: Make his road home a long one

effects.log: Foxfire in the reeds, a lantern that goes the wrong way, a bridge that is not where he left it. He comes home three days late, half drowned and grey in the face, and never wears the cap again. Neither does he forget. Neither do you.

events.text: A moneylender lodges with you on a collecting round. You have heard the stories in three villages: the fields taken, the daughters sent into service, the old man who hanged his debts round his own neck. He sleeps soundly in your best room. If anyone deserves to wake up pale, the bead whispers, it is him.

choices.text: Remember that the vow does not say "anyone who does not deserve it"

effects.log: No harm to anyone. Not anyone except. The old rules were made by foxes who knew exactly how this argument goes, and closed the door on it. You lie awake and let him sleep.

choices.text: Burn his ledger in the brazier instead

effects.log: It goes up beautifully. In the morning he screams the house down, and three villages are free of him for a year while he rebuilds the books from memory, badly. Is a ledger harm? The moon, apparently, does not think so.

choices.text: Draw the thread. He of all people

effects.log: He is pale and frightened all the way round his circuit, and collects nothing, and the villages bless the fever. The vow is broken anyway. It turns out the moon does not care whose breath it was.

events.text: A full moon in a hungry year. Your bead has gone dull as a river stone, and a band of pilgrims is asleep in the lee of the grave mounds with their straw hats over their faces: eleven sleepers, eleven warm breaths, and the nearest is close enough to touch with your tail.

choices.text: Bow to the moon all night instead, on the far side of the hill

effects.log: Eleven sleepers on one side of the hill, you and the moon on the other. By dawn the bead is a shade brighter, the slow way. The pilgrims go on toward the temple without knowing they were ever counted.

choices.text: Lead them in the morning to a good spring and a dry road

effects.log: A light on the path at dawn, always just ahead. They follow it to a spring they did not know was there. The oldest pilgrim bows toward the hill before they go. Something in the bead warms, a little, at that.

choices.text: Take one thread from the nearest. Only one

effects.log: Only one, from the nearest, and the bead brightens so fast it hurts. The pilgrim stumbles all the next day and is carried by the others. Only one. It is always only one.

events.text: The old fox of the hill comes to your mound in the shape of an old woman in a hat that is not a hat, as it did when you were a kit. "A thousand days," it says. "I tried it twice. There is a quicker way, the old way, which the stories name and I will not, here, in front of the dead. Come with me one night and I will show you."

choices.text: Send it away

effects.log: "Go home," you say, "and take the hat." It laughs, a dry sound like leaves, and goes. At the bottom of the hill it turns and calls back that it will ask again in a hundred years. It will, too.

choices.text: Let it talk all night, and refuse at dawn

effects.log: It tells you everything except the one thing, which it will not say on a grave. You listen to all of it. At dawn you say no. It is not the same as never having listened, and you both know it.

choices.text: Go with it, one night

effects.log: You go with it, one night, to a place the stories name and this one will not. You come back at dawn with a bead like a small sun and a silence in you that does not go. The vow is broken. That is the least of it.

events.text: A bandit falls against your door in a blizzard with an arrow wound in the thigh, and passes out on the step. There is a price on his head in two counties. He is breathing hard and warm, and he would die in the snow if you left him there, and nobody in the world would ask you why.

choices.text: Drag him in and dress the wound

effects.log: He wakes on your floor three days later and looks at you as if you were a ghost. When he can walk he goes, without a word, and in the spring you find a pheasant hung on your gate. Bandits have manners, sometimes.

choices.text: Carry him to the temple gate down the valley

effects.log: A long way in the snow with a heavy man over your shoulder. The monks take him in. Whether they hand him over for the price is their business. Not harm, on your side of the ledger. Not much else, either.

choices.text: Take what breath he has left; he will not miss it

effects.log: He would have lived. That is the thing you know as you walk away from the step with the bead blazing. He would have lived, and now nobody will ever know whether he would have, and the vow is broken.

events.text: A young swordsman with too much pride has heard that the keeper of this house was once seen to move faster than a person moves. He wants a bout, here, now, in the yard, in front of his friends. He will not take no for an answer, and his friends are already making a ring.

choices.text: Refuse, and keep refusing until they get bored

effects.log: An hour of being called a coward in your own yard. In the end the friends drift off, and the swordsman with them, muttering. A thousand days is mostly this: being called things, and letting them stand.

choices.text: Fight like the person you pretend to be: slow, and badly, and lose

ok.log: You manage to lose convincingly, which is harder than winning. He goes away satisfied that the stories were nonsense. Nobody is hurt, least of all the vow.

fail.log: You lose rather more convincingly than you meant to. A cracked rib, a cut lip, and a swordsman who is very pleased with himself. The vow holds. Your ribs disagree about whether it was worth it. (-12 health)

choices.text: Win with the Stolen Breath, the fox's way

effects.log: His rhythm is yours across the space between you, and his breath with it. He goes down pale and does not know how. His friends saw something, and do not know what. The vow broke at the first touch of that thread.

events.text: The dog next door has decided, after years of peace, that it knows what you are. It barks every time you cross the yard, and its master has begun to look at you over the fence the way men look at a sky before hail. One night the master falls asleep on his own step, waiting up for the dog to explain itself.

choices.text: Make friends with the dog, one bone at a time

effects.log: A season of bones over the fence, and the dog decides that whatever you are, you are generous. The master stops watching the sky. A dog that loves a fox is still a dog that knows. It just stops saying so.

choices.text: Hide the tails all season and go the long way round

effects.log: No lamps, no yard, the back lane and the long way. The dog barks at nothing for a month and its master decides the dog is getting old. It is not the dog that is old.

choices.text: Draw a thread from the master as he sleeps, so he forgets

effects.log: He wakes pale on his own step and cannot remember why he was waiting. The dog remembers. It barks all winter. The vow is broken, and the dog was right, and you have proved it.

events.text: A spring hunger in the hills. The villages are eating pine bark boiled soft and the roots of kudzu. Under the snow by the stream lies a deer that died of the cold, and a starving family has seen it too; you can hear them coming up the slope with a sledge, slowly, because they are weak. You are hungry too, and you are faster.

choices.text: Leave the deer and go back up the hill

effects.log: You watch from the pines while they load it, crying, onto the sledge. A hungry spring. You catch a vole on the way home and it is enough, nearly. (-5 health)

choices.text: Drag it down to their path so they do not have to climb

effects.log: They come round the bend and find it lying in the path as if laid there, and look up the slope at the pines, and say a word that is not quite thanks and not quite prayer. You are already gone.

events.text: {npc} has come to your door every day for six years: first for the thing you sell, then for the talk, then for no reason at all. Tonight {he} does not leave when the lamp is lit. {He} sits on the porch turning a cup round and round, and then says it plainly, the way {he} says everything: {he} would like to share a house with the person you are. Not this year, if you need time. But {he} would like to.
events.arc: The One Who Loves the Mask

choices.text: Say yes

effects.log: {npc} lets out a breath {he} has been holding for six years and laughs at {him}self for it. You laugh too. Inside you, every tail goes very still, the way a fox goes still in long grass when the dogs pass close.

choices.text: Say yes, on one condition you will name later

effects.log: "Any condition," {npc} says at once, and then, more carefully, "Within reason." You promise it will be within reason. You are not sure that is true. A fox's reasons are not a person's.

choices.text: Say no, gently, and mean it kindly

effects.log: {npc} nods, and finishes the cup, and goes home. {He} still comes every day, for the talk. It is a good deal more than most foxes get, and a good deal less than you wanted.

events.text: Years of an ordinary house. {npc} snores a little and pretends not to. The kimchi jars on the terrace are opened in the right order. The mending is done on winter evenings, side by side, with the lamp between you, and {he} talks about the neighbours while you sit with your back to the wall so your shadow falls where nobody looks.
events.arc: The One Who Loves the Mask

choices.text: Learn to make the soup {his} family made

effects.log: It takes you nine tries. On the ninth {npc} puts down the spoon and does not say anything for a while. Then {he} asks for more. You have hunted hares that were less difficult.

choices.text: Keep the lamp always on your own side of the room

effects.log: It becomes a small habit of the house, like the jars. {npc} teases you about it: you like the lamp close, you are always cold. You let {him} think so. It is almost true.

choices.text: Let {him} see you laugh, really laugh, once

effects.log: Something {he} says about the neighbour's goat. You laugh with your whole face, and for one breath your eyes catch the lamp the way a fox's do. {npc} blinks. Then {he} laughs too, and decides {he} imagined it.

events.text: There is one thing you have to ask, and you have put it off three winters. In the old stories the fox asks it on the first night, and the stories never say what it cost to ask. You sit with {npc} on the porch after the harvest, and the words are there in your mouth with the bead.
events.arc: The One Who Loves the Mask

choices.text: "For a hundred nights, do not look at me while I sleep"

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long while. "That is a strange thing to ask," {he} says. "I will do it. Will you tell me why, after?" You say yes. You do not know whether you are lying. Neither, from {his} face, does {he}.

choices.text: Ask nothing, and sleep in the other room "for the cold"

effects.log: The other room is colder, which makes no sense, and {npc} says so. You say you like the cold. {He} lets it go. It is a small lie on top of the large one, and it sits badly.

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth: what you are, and how many tails

effects.log: You tell it all, from the earth under the mound to the last tail. {npc} does not run. {He} sits a long time, and then asks, very practically, whether you eat the same rice. You do. "Then nothing has to change," {he} says, and is wrong, and is kind.

events.text: Some night past the sixtieth of the hundred. You wake in the dark because the lamp has been lit. {npc} is sitting up on the other side of the paper screen with the lamp in {his} hand, and the light is coming through the paper onto you, and {his} shadow is very still. {He} has not looked yet. {He} is deciding.
events.arc: The One Who Loves the Mask

choices.text: Speak first, softly: "Please."

effects.log: The shadow on the screen flinches. Then the lamp goes out. In the morning neither of you mentions it, and {npc} makes the soup the way you learned it, without being asked.

choices.text: Lie still, and trust {him}

ok.log: A long time. Then the lamp goes out, and you hear {npc} lie down again, and breathe, and after a while sleep. {He} did not look. You lie awake till dawn with the bead warm in your mouth, and something in you that was a fox for centuries learns a new thing.

fail.log: The screen slides a finger's width. One breath of lamplight, one look, and then it slides shut again. In the morning {npc} is very quiet and very kind, and does not ask you anything, and you do not know what {he} saw.

choices.text: Turn over three times in the dark and be only a person

effects.log: When the light comes through the paper there is nothing on the mat but a person asleep. It costs the bead something, and it costs you something else. {npc} puts out the lamp, ashamed. The trick worked. You are not sure that is a good thing.

events.text: {npc}'s old mother comes to live with you after a bad winter, and sits in the warmest corner, and watches you eat. The old mother has seen a great many things, and is not in a hurry, and on the third evening says to the room: "In my village we used to say: count the shadows when the lamp is lit."
events.arc: The One Who Loves the Mask

choices.text: Laugh, and ask what else they used to say in that village

effects.log: A great deal, it turns out: about salt peddlers, about yellow dogs, about the fox that lived in the big grave on the hill. You listen to all of it with great interest. The old mother watches you listen. Neither of you blinks first.

choices.text: Win the old mother over with a winter of small kindnesses

effects.log: Hot stones for the bed, the softest rice, the stories asked for twice. In spring the old mother says to {npc}, in your hearing: "Whatever it is, it is good to you." {npc} does not understand. You do.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to send the old mother to a cousin

effects.log: {npc} does it, unhappily. The house is easier, and colder. The old mother goes without a fuss, and at the gate turns and says only, "Look after my child." You do. You owed that much.

events.text: Long years. {npc} is grey now and stiff in the mornings, and you are not. The neighbours have started to remark on it, admiringly: the keeper of that house must eat well. {npc} has stopped remarking on it at all, which is worse. One evening {he} holds up the bronze mirror between your two faces and looks at it for a long time.
events.arc: The One Who Loves the Mask

choices.text: Age your borrowed face, a little each year, with the bead

effects.log: A line at the eye, grey at the temple, a stiffness you have to remember to perform. It costs bead every year to grow old beside someone. {npc} puts the mirror away and never takes it out again.

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth, if {he} does not know it already

effects.log: "I know," {npc} says, before you are halfway through. "I have known since the soup." {He} puts the mirror down. "I only wanted you to say it to me once while I could still hear properly."

choices.text: Let {him} wonder, and say nothing

effects.log: {npc} puts the mirror down without a word. After that {he} sometimes watches you across the room as if trying to remember a word in another language. You let {him}. It is a cruelty, small and daily, and you know it.

events.text: {npc} is dying, old and unafraid, in the room with the lamp. {He} sends everyone out but you, and takes your hand, and says: "I looked once. Years ago, one night in the middle of the hundred. I saw them, all of them, lying across the mat like a fan. Then I put the lamp out and went back to sleep. I wanted you to know I kept the rest of the nights."
events.arc: The One Who Loves the Mask

choices.text: Say thank you, and nothing else

effects.log: It is the right thing to say. {npc} smiles and goes to sleep holding your hand and does not wake. You sit with {him} till dawn with the lamp lit and your shadow on the wall, all of it, for anyone to see.

choices.text: Tell {him} your true name, the one from the earth under the mound

effects.log: It is not a human name. It is a sound a vixen made in the dark centuries ago. {npc} tries to say it back and nearly manages, and laughs, and that is the last sound {he} makes.

choices.text: Let the shadow show, so the last thing {he} sees is the truth

effects.log: You move the lamp so it is behind you. Every tail you have, on the wall. {npc} looks at them a long time, with great interest, like a farmer looking at a good field. "There," {he} says. "That is better."

events.text: Your borrowed face has done too well. A provincial governor writes to the capital about the person in his county who cures what no one else can, reads what no one else reads, and never seems tired. A palace messenger arrives on a lathered horse with a summons sealed in red. The court wants you. It does not say for what. All those tails, and a palace full of lamps and dogs.

choices.text: Go as a court physician

effects.log: The physicians' office gives you a dark robe and a cramped room by the herb store, and a king's pulse to take on the third day. It is slow and frightened. You know the feeling.

choices.text: Go as a minister's secretary

effects.log: A minister of the second rank wants someone who can write a fair hand and keep a secret. You can do both better than anyone alive. By winter you have read every letter that crosses his desk.

choices.text: Go as an attendant in the palace

effects.log: The lowest post, the quietest one: lamps, doors, the long corridors at night. Nobody looks at the person who trims the wicks. You see everything.

choices.text: Send back word that you are ill, and stay where you are

effects.log: The messenger goes back with a letter about a weak chest. The court forgets you in a month. Your village does not; they had a feast for the letter.

events.text: The king sends for you at the hour of the rat, when the palace is dark. He sits alone behind the screen with one lamp, and asks you, of all the people in the palace, what he should do about the river: the dykes in the south have burst, and the ministers say rebuild the royal tombs first, for luck.

choices.text: Tell him the truth: rice before tombs

effects.log: He listens without moving. The next morning the tomb works are stopped and the labourers sent south to the dykes. Three ministers want to know who spoke to the king at night. They begin to find out.

choices.text: Tell him what he wants to hear, and keep your place

effects.log: The tombs are rebuilt, beautifully. In the south the rice rots in the water. The king thanks you for your counsel and sends you a bolt of silk. You give the silk away and cannot get the smell of the flood out of your nose.

choices.text: Say you are only a servant and know nothing of rivers

effects.log: He looks at you a long while, and lets you go. "Everyone in this palace knows nothing of rivers," he says to the lamp. You go out with your back to the light, so the shadow falls behind you, where kings do not look.

events.text: There is a monk at court whom the king trusts above all his ministers: born, they whisper, to a temple slave, risen from nothing, who eats black chickens and white horses and is afraid of yellow dogs. The ministers call him the old fox. He is not a fox. You would know. He is only a clever, frightened man with too many enemies, and the court is looking for a fox to burn.

choices.text: Defend him quietly, in the right ears

effects.log: A word in the king's ear, a letter misfiled, a witness who remembers differently. The monk keeps his place another year. One evening he passes you in the corridor and says, very low, "It takes one to know one, they say." He does not know how right he is.

choices.text: Let the court have its old fox, and keep your own tails hidden

effects.log: They hunt him down within the year. You watch the sentence read out in the courtyard. Every eye in the palace is on him; none is on you. It is the safest you have been since you came, and you cannot eat for a month.

choices.text: Warn him in secret to leave the capital

effects.log: A note in his sleeve, in a hand he does not know. He reads it, and laughs, and stays. Clever men always stay. You did what you could, and it was not enough, and you knew it would not be.

events.text: {npc}, a minister of the third rank with ink on {his} cuffs, has started arriving early and leaving late, and always seems to be in the corridor when you pass the lamps. Tonight {he} is waiting at the turning, alone, and says without preamble: "Your shadow is wrong. I have been counting for a year. I am not going to tell anyone. I want to know why you came."

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth: to learn what people are

effects.log: {npc} listens with {his} hands in {his} sleeves. "And what are they?" {he} asks. "Frightened, mostly," you say. "Kind more often than they need to be." {He} nods, as at a good report, and keeps your secret for the rest of {his} life.

choices.text: Ask {him} why {he} has not told anyone

effects.log: "Because you are the only person in this palace who has never asked me for anything," {npc} says. "I find I do not want to lose that." It is the oddest friendship of your long life, and one of the best.

choices.text: Have {him} sent to a post in the far north

effects.log: A word in the king's ear, and {npc} is governor of a frontier county by spring. {He} goes without protest. At the gate {he} bows to you, very correctly, and you understand that {he} would have kept the secret anyway.

events.text: A prince of the blood has been given a yellow dog from the north, a big rangy hound with a nose like a lantern, and walks it through the palace every morning. The first time it sees you it stops dead in the corridor and lays its ears flat and makes a sound in its chest like a drum. The prince laughs. Then he stops laughing.

choices.text: Kneel and offer the dog your open hand

ok.log: The dog sniffs your hand a long time. Then it sits, and sighs, and leans its whole weight against your knee. The prince is enchanted. "It has never done that for anyone," he says. Dogs know. Some of them also forgive.

fail.log: The dog takes your sleeve and very nearly your hand. The prince hauls it off, white. All day the corridor talks about the hound that hates the new physician. (-6 health)

choices.text: Arrange never to be in the same corridor again

effects.log: A season of routes: the back stairs, the kitchen court, the long way through the archive. You become an expert in the palace's plumbing. The dog grows old looking for you.

choices.text: Tell the prince, laughing, that the dog smells the herbs on you

effects.log: "Wolf-bane," you say, "and a little valerian. Dogs hate it." The prince believes you. The dog does not. Every morning it sits in the corridor and watches your door, patient as a tax collector.

events.text: The king who listened to you at night is dead, and the new king is young and does not sleep with a lamp. The court that knew your face is turning over like soil in spring. The dog in the corridor is old. You have been here longer than anyone notices, and soon someone will.

choices.text: Stay, and teach the young king what the old one learned

effects.log: He is impatient and quick, and he learns. Some nights he asks, half joking, how old you are. You say you lost count. It is the only lie you tell him.

choices.text: Retire to the country with an herb stall, and leave the court your advice in writing

effects.log: A long memorial on rivers, granaries and dogs, left on the young king's desk. Then an ox cart, a village with a well, and a waiting room full of people who cannot pay. It is a good face. It always was.

choices.text: Stay, and steer the young king toward your own ends

effects.log: He is easy to steer, which is the problem. By the third year the court calls you what they called the monk. They are right this time. You find you do not mind as much as you should.

events.text: A kingdom is failing. You can smell it from the hills the way you smell rain: the granaries half empty, the frontier forts unpaid, the king feasting while the river towns pay twice. In the second month of spring the young foxes of the hills begin to go down into the capital at night, by the drains and over the walls, as if called. The palace guards chase them through the gardens with torches.
events.arc: The White Fox on the Desk

choices.text: Go down and see for yourself

effects.log: You go over the wall at the hour of the ox. Fox-prints in the frost of the throne courtyard, fox-prints round the treasury. Something in the old earth under the palace is calling the foxes in, the way a carcass calls crows.

choices.text: Lead the young foxes back out to the hills

effects.log: Foxfire at the drains, night after night, leading them out. Some follow. Some do not. A palace that has foxes in it in spring is a palace the histories will write about, and you would rather it were not your kin they write about.

choices.text: Stay on the mound and keep out of it

effects.log: Kingdoms fall. You have seen two go already. You stay on the hill and bow to the moon, and listen to the dogs of the capital barking all spring.

events.text: Late one night the chief minister's hall stands open, the lamps out, the desk bare but for a stack of memorials that nobody has read. You stand in the doorway. Everyone in the palace knows what it would mean: a fox on the minister's desk, in plain sight, in spring. The old histories are full of it. You could write yourself into them.
events.arc: The White Fox on the Desk

choices.text: Climb up and sit on the desk until the morning bell

effects.log: You sit with your tails folded round your feet on the chief minister's memorials. At the morning bell a clerk opens the door and drops a tray of ink. You look at him. Then you get down, and walk out past him, slowly, so everyone in the corridor sees.

choices.text: Read the memorials instead, and leave them in a better order

effects.log: Reports of famine, of unpaid soldiers, of a governor selling posts. You put the worst on top. In the morning the chief minister finds them so, and goes white, and nobody can explain it.

choices.text: Go in a borrowed face, and warn the king in words

effects.log: You stand before the screen and say what a fox would say if it sat on the desk: mend the granaries, pay the forts, stop the feasts. The king listens politely and goes to the feast. You were a sign; he did not read it.

events.text: The court meets about the fox. The astronomers say a white fox on the desk means the minister must resign. The shamans say it means the gods are watching. The chief minister says it means somebody let a fox in. The king laughs and says a fox is a fox, and calls for wine. Only one young official in the back row is silent, writing.
events.arc: The White Fox on the Desk

choices.text: Find the young official, and tell {him} what the sign really means

effects.log: A voice at {npc}'s window at night: the granaries, the forts, the feasts. {He} does not ask who you are. {He} writes it all down in a memorial so plain that the king has {him} sent to the provinces for impertinence. {He} goes, and writes it again from there.

choices.text: Come again, the next night, to the king's own table

effects.log: You walk across the banquet hall between the dancers in plain sight, tails and all, and sit for one breath at the end of the king's table. Then you are gone. Nobody laughs this time. Nobody does anything, either. That is the worst of it.

choices.text: Leave them to their meeting; you have done enough

effects.log: A sign is a sign. What a court does with it is the court's business. You go back to the hills and do not watch, and hear about it anyway from every pedlar on the road.

events.text: Some years later the enemy's armies are across the river, and the court is packing its seals into ox carts. The palace women are burning letters. In the servants' quarters, nobody has thought about the children of the cooks and the grooms, who have nowhere to go and no carts to go in.
events.arc: The White Fox on the Desk

choices.text: Lead the servants' children out over the hills by foxfire

effects.log: A light ahead of them for three nights, always just far enough. They follow it to a village in the hills that the armies never reach. Years later they tell their own children about the lantern that walked by itself, and the fox they sometimes saw holding it.

choices.text: Go to the minister's hall one more time, to see it empty

effects.log: The desk is still there. The memorials are gone, burned or packed. You sit on it once more in the smoke, and nobody comes. A kingdom ending is quieter than you thought.

choices.text: Go home to the mound and let it end

effects.log: You go up the hill against the stream of refugees coming down. Nobody looks at a fox going the wrong way. From the mound you watch the capital's lamps go out, one quarter at a time.

events.text: The last spring. The plum is in flower in the empty palace, the enemy is at the gates, and the king has fled by the north road. The chief minister's hall is open to the wind. Somebody will write this spring down, and what they write will be read for a thousand years. You know, standing in the doorway, that you could be in it.
events.arc: The White Fox on the Desk

choices.text: Go out through the plum garden and up into the hills

effects.log: You go out past the blossom without stopping, and up into the hills, and do not look back at the smoke. Another dynasty will build on these stones. You will see it. Signs are for people who end; you do not end here.

choices.text: Stay in the city in a borrowed face and help with what comes after

effects.log: The soldiers come in, and then the officials of the new order, and then the hungry. Somebody has to keep a pot on the fire at the crossroads. For years, somebody does.

choices.text: Climb onto the desk again and stay there, and be the sign for ever

effects.log: You climb up onto the lacquered desk in the empty hall, in plain sight, with the plum blowing in at the door, and you stay. The first soldiers through the gate find you there, and stop, and do not come closer. The histories still have you: the kingdom's last spring, and a fox on the minister's desk.

events.text: Autumn, the seventh month. A king hunts on the plain below your ridge with a hundred riders, and you can smell him from the hill: wine, old blood, and a fear that is not of deer. In the low gold light your coat looks pale as frost. Something in the bead aches at the sight of him, and before you know it you are running along the ridge after the hunt, crying out as foxes cry.
events.arc: The King Who Killed the Shaman

choices.text: Follow the hunt, crying, in plain sight

effects.log: All afternoon, along the ridge, a pale fox crying after the king. The riders point. The king reins in, and looks up at you, and his face goes very still. Then he calls for his bow.

choices.text: Stop yourself and go to ground

effects.log: You lie in the silver grass with your heart going like a drum until the hunt is past. Whatever the bead wanted to say to that king, it will have to say another way, or not at all.

choices.text: Sit on the highest rock, silent, and let him see you

effects.log: You do not cry. You sit. That is worse. The king sees a pale fox watching him from the rock all afternoon, never moving, and the hunt goes home early with nothing.

events.text: The king's arrow goes past your ear into the grass. He calls for the court shaman, an old man in white with bells at his wrists. The shaman looks at you a long time and says: "A fox is an uncanny beast and no good sign. But if the king mends his virtue, the ill can turn to fortune." The king says: "If it is ill, say ill. If good, say good. First uncanny and then fortune: what lie is this?" And the guards take the old man away.
events.arc: The King Who Killed the Shaman

choices.text: Run down after the guards, and lead the shaman off into the reeds

ok.log: Foxfire in the reed beds at dusk, three guards chasing lights, and one old man in white who understands at once and runs the other way. He is gone over the river by moonrise. The king tells the court the shaman was executed. The shaman, three villages away, tells everyone otherwise.

fail.log: Too many guards, too much open ground. An arrow takes you along the flank, and by the time you are up again the old man is gone, and the king has made his point to his court. You hear the bells stop. (-8 health)

choices.text: Cry out once more, so the court remembers what the shaman said

effects.log: One long cry from the ridge as they lead him off. Every rider in the hunt hears it, and every one of them remembers the old man's words: mend your virtue. The king does not mend his. Some of his riders do.

choices.text: Turn away. You did this

effects.log: You go back over the ridge with the sound of the bells behind you. A fox cried, a shaman spoke honestly, a king did what kings do. Only one of the three could have chosen otherwise, and it was not the shaman.

events.text: The shaman's family lives in a hut at the edge of the capital: a grown daughter who keeps the bells now, and a grandchild of six. The court has taken their rice ration, and the neighbours are afraid to be seen with them. The bells hang on the door, silent.
events.arc: The King Who Killed the Shaman

choices.text: Bring them rice in a borrowed face, every month, and say nothing

effects.log: A pedlar who comes on the first of every month, leaves a sack, and will not be paid. The daughter thinks it is a cousin of her father's. The grandchild watches you go every time, all the way to the bend, very carefully.

choices.text: Leave a hare on their step at night, as a fox would

effects.log: A hare, a pheasant, once a whole wild goose. The daughter finds them in the mornings and looks up at the hills, and rings her father's bells once, softly. You hear it on the ridge.

choices.text: Ask the daughter to read your fortune

effects.log: She shakes the bells and throws the rice and looks at the grains, and then at you. "You are carrying something that is not yours," she says. "Put it down where you found it." She does not take your coin.

events.text: The king who killed the shaman rules badly and long. Taxes double. A loyal minister is exiled for a joke. In the palace a quiet official of the old court, a man no one fears, has begun to meet other quiet men at night. You know what they are planning; you can smell it on them, like rain coming.
events.arc: The King Who Killed the Shaman

choices.text: Help them: foxfire to lead the guards the wrong way on the night

effects.log: On the night, every guard in the eastern court follows a light round the same pond three times. By morning there is a new king. Nobody ever knows why the guards were in the wrong place. The shaman would have said: a fox is no good sign. He would have been right.

choices.text: Stay out of it; this is human business

effects.log: You keep to the hills. The king falls anyway, the next year, the way kings like that fall. You hear it from a pedlar on the road and feel nothing in particular, and that worries you a little.

choices.text: Go to the king once more, crying on the ridge, to give him one last chance

effects.log: He hears you. He comes out onto the palace wall and looks at the ridge for a long time. Then he goes in and calls for wine. The quiet men act within the month. You gave him the chance. He did not want it.

events.text: Decades on. A shaman in white with old bells at the wrists comes up the hill road and stops at your grave mound and sits down on the grass, uninvited, as if visiting a relative. It is the grandchild, grown old. "My grandfather's fox," the old shaman says to the mound. "I always knew which hill. Tell me: was he right? Ill, or fortune?"
events.arc: The King Who Killed the Shaman

choices.text: Come out, and say: "Both. That was the truth of it"

effects.log: The old shaman nods slowly, as if a debt had been paid, and rings the bells once. "That is what I tell people," the shaman says. "Nobody likes it." You sit together on the mound till dusk, two old things who told a king the truth.

choices.text: Stay in the earth and let the bells do the asking

effects.log: The shaman rings and waits, rings and waits, and at dusk leaves a cup of rice wine on the mound and goes. At midnight you breathe in the smell of it and leave it for the dead. It is the best gift you have ever been given, and it is not because of the wine.

events.text: An old monk in a patched grey robe sits down beside you at a ferry landing on the west coast, where nobody else will sit, and says without looking at you: "Six. I have seven, though I keep them very tidy." He smells of salt and incense and fox. "I keep a hermitage on an island two days out. There is a pool there with a dragon family in it, and a dragon keeps what we want inside it. Come and share."
events.arc: The Monk on the West Sea Island

choices.text: Go with him on the next boat, to see

effects.log: Two days on a fishing boat that he pays for with a blessing. The island is black rock and wind and one stunted pine. He shows you the hermitage, which is a cave, and the pool, which is very deep, and smiles like an uncle.

choices.text: Refuse, and ask him what dragons ever did to him

effects.log: "Lived," he says. "Very long, very well, with a great deal of light inside them." He gets on the boat alone and tells you the name of the island, in case you change your mind. You will remember it.

choices.text: Go with him, and warn the sea at the first chance

effects.log: On the boat you drop a pine needle into the sea with a word folded in it, the way your aunt taught you to send word to water. Whether the sea reads, you will find out.

events.text: Dawn on the island. The old monk stands on the rock above the pool and begins to chant, a dharani you do not know, very fast and very low. The water heaves. Shapes rise in it, blue-green and long, an old dragon and his wife and their sons, lifted helpless to the surface and turning there like leaves in a millrace. "Now," the monk says, without stopping. "Chant with me, and take your share."
events.arc: The Monk on the West Sea Island

choices.text: Chant with him

effects.log: You learn the words in three breaths. The pool groans. When the sun clears the sea the dragons sink back into the dark, weaker than they rose, and the monk hands you something that the old way names and this story will not. The bead is brighter. You are not.

choices.text: Stand and watch, and do nothing

effects.log: You watch it all. The monk does not mind; he thinks you are shy. As the dragons sink back the old one looks up at you from the water, once, and you understand that dragons remember faces.

choices.text: Break his chant: knock him off the rock

ok.log: You hit him from behind with all six tails. The chant breaks; the dragons drop into the dark. He gets up spitting salt, and looks at you with seven tails bristling, and laughs. "Tomorrow, then," he says. "And the day after."

fail.log: Seven tails beat six. He throws you down on the rock without missing a syllable, and finishes the dawn. Afterwards he dresses your scrapes like an uncle and says you will learn. (-16 health)

events.text: A ship of the court's envoys to the western empire put in at the island for a storm and has left without one of its men: an archer, by the look of the bow, marooned on a rock by lot to appease the sea. He has a bow, nine arrows, and no food. He sits by the dragon pool looking at the water as if it had said something to him in the night.
events.arc: The Monk on the West Sea Island

choices.text: Lead him to the spring and the gulls' eggs with foxfire

effects.log: A light on the rocks at dusk, always ahead. He follows it to fresh water and a ledge of eggs and lives. He knows the light is something. He is too polite, or too hungry, to ask what.

choices.text: Keep out of his sight; it is the monk's island

effects.log: You keep to the far side of the rock. He finds the spring himself on the third day, half dead. Archers are hard to kill, it turns out. You should have remembered that.

choices.text: Sit where he can see you, and look at the pool, and then at him

effects.log: He looks at you, and at the pool, and at the old monk's cave, for a long time. Then he strings his bow. Archers are not stupid either.

events.text: The old fox-monk is restless. "The archer dreams," he tells you over his gruel. "The old dragon walks into his sleep and begs. I can smell it on him in the mornings." He puts down his bowl. "Tomorrow at dawn I finish it: the old dragon, his wife, his sons, all of them. Stand beside me. Seven and six, nobody can stop thirteen."
events.arc: The Monk on the West Sea Island

choices.text: Promise to stand beside him

effects.log: "Good," he says, and pats your head as if you were a kit again. You lie awake all night on the cold rock listening to the sea, and to the archer, on the other side of the island, oiling his bowstring.

choices.text: Refuse him, plainly

effects.log: "Then stay out of the way," he says, not unkindly, and goes to sleep at once, like the very old. You do not sleep at all.

choices.text: Warn him: the archer is ready, and the dragon has asked

effects.log: He laughs. "An arrow," he says, "against a dharani." He has been alive four hundred years longer than you, and he has never once been wrong about a human. You think he is about to be.

events.text: Dawn. The monk climbs the rock above the pool and begins the dharani. The water heaves and the dragons rise. On the ledge below, the archer draws. You have the space of one breath, the way a fox always has, between the string going back and the arrow going.
events.arc: The Monk on the West Sea Island

choices.text: Stand back on the cliff and let the arrow fly

effects.log: The string sings. The chant stops in the middle of a word. Something falls from the rock into the shallows, and it is not a monk, and it is not anything any more. You go down later and lay the grey robe over it. Nobody else on the island ever will.

choices.text: Drag the old monk off the rock before the string goes

ok.log: You hit him at the knees and you both go over the back of the rock into the heather, and the arrow goes over your heads into the sea. The dragons sink. He lies there cursing you in three languages. He is alive. He never chants on that island again.

fail.log: He throws you off with seven tails and the arrow takes him in the throat of his chant. He falls as what he was. You lie on the rock with your ribs broken and the sea very loud. (-15 health)

choices.text: Climb up and chant beside the old monk to the end, as you promised

effects.log: You take your place beside him on the rock and open your mouth on the dharani. The arrow comes out of the sunrise. Then a second one. You fall together into the shallow water at the pool's edge, two old foxes, and the dragons sink back into the dark, and the archer lowers the bow and goes to tell the sea it is done.

events.text: Months later, a ship comes back for the archer. He goes down to it with a flower in his collar, a strange white flower that does not wilt, which he keeps touching as if it might speak. On the beach he stops, and looks up at the cliff where you are, and lifts his bow to you, very slightly, as a soldier salutes.
events.arc: The Monk on the West Sea Island

choices.text: Lift your tails to him in answer

effects.log: All your tails against the sky. The sailors on the ship see it and make the sign against evil. The archer does not. He has had a strange year and decided, it seems, that not everything on the cliff is an enemy.

choices.text: Go down to the pool and look into it before you leave the island

effects.log: Deep water, very still. Then far down a blue-green eye opens and looks at you, and closes again. Dragons remember faces. For once you are glad of it.

events.text: A famine year. You come up to your own mound at dusk and there is a bundle on it, wrapped in a hemp jacket that was somebody's best: a baby, very quiet, too hungry to cry. Somebody left it on the grave mound with the fox in it, because the old people say a fox in a grave keeps the grave lucky, and nobody else could keep it at all.
events.arc: The Child at the Grave Mound

choices.text: Take the child home to your borrowed face

effects.log: You carry {npc} down to the house in the dark. The neighbours are told it is a cousin's child from the next valley. They count on their fingers and say nothing. In a famine year nobody asks where a child came from; only whether there is rice.

choices.text: Carry the child to the temple gate down the valley

effects.log: The monks open the gate at dawn and find the bundle, and a fox sitting a little way off, watching. The fox leaves when the gate shuts. The child grows up a novice, and never knows.

choices.text: Leave the child at the door of a house that has no children

effects.log: A childless pair of rice farmers, kind and sad. In the morning there is a shriek, and then a different kind of shriek. You go away up the hill. It was a good door. You chose it carefully.

events.text: {npc} is small, and fast. Faster than a child should be: {he} catches a sparrow in the yard with both hands and brings it to you to show, and lets it go. The neighbours' dog, which barks at everyone, lies down and whines when {npc} goes by. You did not do anything to {him}. You think. You are not sure what a child absorbs from a house where the shadows are wrong.
events.arc: The Child at the Grave Mound

choices.text: Teach {him} to be slow in front of other people

effects.log: A game: who can walk to the well the slowest. {npc} wins every time, scowling with concentration. You know exactly what you are teaching, and why. It is the first lesson you ever had too.

choices.text: Let {him} be as fast as {he} is

effects.log: {npc} runs everywhere, catches everything, falls out of every tree and is never hurt. The village starts telling stories. You let them. A child should not have to hide what {he} is. One of you in the house is enough.

choices.text: Sit {him} on the grave mound at the full moon, just once

effects.log: {npc} sits beside you on the grass and looks at the moon with {his} mouth open and asks if it is warm. You say it is. It is not, quite. It is the truest lie you have told in a hundred years.

events.text: The children of the village have found a word for {npc}: fox-born. They chant it in the lane. {npc} comes home with a cut lip, having fought four of them at once and won, and sits on the step and asks you, very seriously, whether it is true.
events.arc: The Child at the Grave Mound

choices.text: "Somebody left you on a fox's grave. That is all it means"

effects.log: It is true, and it is not the whole truth. {npc} thinks about it and decides it is a good story, and the next time the children chant it, {he} chants it back, louder. They stop.

choices.text: "Being fox-born is no shame. Foxes are clever, and loyal"

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time with eyes that catch the lamp, as yours do. "Loyal to who?" {he} asks. "To whoever raised them," you say. {He} nods, satisfied. So, strangely, are you.

choices.text: Go and speak to the parents of the four

effects.log: You do not raise your voice. You do not need to. Something in your borrowed face makes four households very quiet and very polite for a year. {npc} is left alone. It is not quite the lesson you meant.

events.text: {npc} is in the thick of growing up. {He} comes down from the hills at dusk with a tiger cub held under one arm like a sack of barley, spitting and clawing, and a scratch down {his} face {he} is very proud of. "Caught it with my hands," {he} says. Up in the hills, very far off, something large begins to roar and does not stop.
events.arc: The Child at the Grave Mound

choices.text: Make {him} carry it back up, right now, with you

effects.log: Up the hill in the dark, the two of you, with the cub and the roaring. You put it down at the edge of the pines and pull {npc} back by the collar, and a great striped shape comes out of the dark and takes it and looks at you both, and goes. (-6 health)

choices.text: Let {him} keep it a night, and learn what it costs

effects.log: By midnight the whole village is barricaded, the dogs gone mad, the roaring at the edge of the fields. {npc} takes the cub back up alone at dawn, white-faced. {He} has learned. So has the village, about the child they call fox-born.

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth about the house, now

effects.log: You take the cub back first. Then, by the lamp, you let {npc} see your shadow as it really is. {He} counts the tails out loud. Then {he} says, "That is why the dog lies down," and laughs until {he} cries, and is not afraid.

events.text: {npc} is grown, and the army is recruiting along the frontier, and {he} wants to go. {He} packs a bundle and sits with you on the porch the last night. "I could catch tigers," {he} says. "They say it. Maybe I could catch other things." A pause. "Whatever happens, I will never hunt on this hill. I wanted you to hear me say it."
events.arc: The Child at the Grave Mound

choices.text: Give {him} your blessing, and nothing else

effects.log: {npc} goes at dawn. You watch from the mound until the road takes {him}. Long years of a borrowed face, kept for one person. It was the best thing you have done with any face.

choices.text: Ask {him} to stay

events.text: Word comes from the frontier the way word does, a pedlar at a time. A young officer who catches tigers with {his} bare hands. events.arc: The Child at the Grave Mound

effects.log: A pedlar at the camp gate, selling needles. {npc} buys a packet without looking up. Then {he} looks up, and goes very still, and pays twice, and says nothing, and you walk away with your heart going like a kit's.

choices.text: Stay on the hill, and listen for news

choices.text: Sit a little way off, every dawn, and breathe with {him}

effects.log: A season of dawns. {npc} never looks at you directly. On the last day of autumn {he} says, to the pine, "Good morning," and you understand that {he} has known all along who {he} was breathing with.

choices.text: Leave chestnuts on {his} step

effects.log: Every morning a little heap of chestnuts, roasted. {npc} eats them gravely and leaves the shells in a neat pile, as rent. Neither of you says anything about it for a year.

choices.text: Test {him}: foxfire round the hermitage at midnight

effects.log: Lights in the trees, voices in the wind. {npc} comes to the door, looks at it all, says "Very pretty," and goes back to bed. You sit in the dark feeling foolish for the first time in centuries.

events.text: A second monk has built a hermitage further up the slope: a sorcerer more than a monk, who drums half the night and burns paper charms and shouts spells at the sky. The birds have left the upper woods. The young monk under your pine sits through it all, very straight, and does not complain, and is getting thin.

choices.text: Go to the sorcerer in the night as a voice, and warn him: move

effects.log: A voice out of the dark beside his drum: "Your noise troubles the one below. Go elsewhere." He stops, and listens, and laughs, and drums louder. That is the first warning.

choices.text: Sit closer to the young monk and share the quiet

effects.log: You lie at the foot of the pine every night, between the hermitage and the drum, and the quiet round {npc} is a little bigger for it. It is not enough. You can feel the mountain getting angry under you.

events.text: The second warning, and the third. The sorcerer has heard the voice twice now, and has decided that it means he is close to something, and drums all night with a sword in his other hand. "Show yourself, spirit," he shouts at the trees. "I am not afraid of a mountain."

choices.text: Show yourself: all your tails in the dark beyond his fire

effects.log: He sees you. He drops the sword, and then picks it up, and then drums faster. Some men are like that: a sign makes them dig in. The mountain shifts under both of you, very slightly.

choices.text: Ask the young monk to go and plead with the sorcerer

effects.log: {npc} goes up the slope with a pot of tea and sits with the sorcerer a whole afternoon. {He} comes back and says only: "That one is frightened of being nobody." The drumming does not stop. But {npc} has tried, and so, now, may you.

choices.text: Warn him the third time in plain words, and mean it

effects.log: "Three times," you say from the dark. "Leave, or the mountain will move you." He laughs. You have done what the old rules ask before a spirit acts. The next thing is the mountain's, and yours.

events.text: The night of the full moon the sorcerer goes down to the village to buy paper for charms. His hermitage is empty. You stand on the slope above it with your tails spread, and feel the whole hillside under you: the wet clay, the loose scree, the old roots that hold it all, and how little it would take.

choices.text: Bring the hillside down on the empty hermitage

effects.log: You pull on the roots. The slope goes with a roar like a river breaking a dam, and the hermitage is under forty feet of earth by moonset. In the morning the sorcerer comes back up the path with his paper, and stands there, and goes away down the mountain shouting. Alive. Furious. Gone.

choices.text: Let the mountain keep still; the drum will stop when he dies

effects.log: You let it be. The drumming goes on for two more winters, until the sorcerer's chest gives out, and the young monk under your pine grows thinner and quieter and never complains. Some patience is only cowardice wearing a robe.

choices.text: Move his drum instead, to the bottom of the valley, every night

effects.log: Every morning his drum is at the bottom of the valley. Every evening he carries it back up. By the second month he is too tired to drum. By the fourth he moves away, cursing the mountain. It is slower than a landslide, and funnier.

events.text: The mountain is quiet again. One dawn you speak to {npc} for the first time in your own voice, from the roots of the pine. "You have learned what this mountain can teach," you say. "Go west across the sea, where the sutras come from, and study. Then come back." {npc} opens {his} eyes and looks straight at you for the first time.

choices.text: Promise to keep {him}: in this life, and the ones after

effects.log: "And I will keep you," {npc} says, as if it were obvious. "Whatever you are, in whatever life." {He} goes down the mountain with a staff and a bowl, west, toward the sea. You sit under the pine and begin to count years.

choices.text: Ask {him} for nothing; only to go

effects.log: {npc} bows to the pine, and then to you. "You ask nothing," {he} says, "so I promise anyway: I will come back, and I will find you, in this life and the ones after." Some promises are made for you whether you want them or not.

choices.text: Tell {him} not to go; the sea is dangerous, and you would miss {him}

effects.log: {npc} stays, out of kindness. {He} grows old under your pine, wise and a little narrow, and never sees the sutras where they come from. You did not want to be alone. It was not a good enough reason.

events.text: Years pass. A monk comes up the path with a staff worn to half its length and a bundle of sutras on {his} back, and sits down under your pine as if {he} had left yesterday. It is {npc}. {He} is weathered, and brown from the western sun, and has a great deal to tell you, and starts at once.

choices.text: Listen to all of it, every word, for a whole season

effects.log: Rivers wider than a province, temples with a thousand rooms, teachers who argued for a month over one word. You listen until the snow. At the end {npc} says, "Now you. What have you been doing?" Waiting, you say. {He} laughs as if that were the best answer.

choices.text: Renew the promise, here, under the pine

effects.log: In this life and the ones after. {npc} says it with you, both hands on the pine's bark. The mountain is very quiet. It is listening too, and it will hold you both to it.

events.text: {npc} is old now, a teacher whom kings send for. On a last visit to the pine {he} asks you, shyly: "In all these years I have never seen what you are. Will you show me? Only once." You think about the tails, the shadow on a paper door. Then you think of something larger.

choices.text: Show {him} an arm reaching out of the clouds to the sky

effects.log: At dawn {npc} looks east and sees it: an arm of mist and pine-shadow reaching up out of the clouds from the mountain to the sky. {He} looks a long time. "Long Arm Mountain," {he} says, and that is what the villages call it from then on.

choices.text: Show {him} the truth: a fox under a pine

effects.log: You come out from the roots and sit in front of {him}, a fox with too many tails. {npc} looks at you with great tenderness. "I thought so," {he} says. "I thought it might be something small." It is the kindest thing anyone has said to you in all your years.

events.text: In the morning the bead does not come back. {npc} swallowed it: you saw {his} throat move in the dark, and then {he} was up and out of the door and running, and fell on the road, and lay there with {his} face to the ground. Half your light has gone into a human. Against your back, one tail folds like a fan closing, and will not open.

choices.text: Follow {him} at once, at a distance

effects.log: You follow {npc} for three days, never close. {He} walks like someone listening to the ground. On the third day {he} stops at a crossroads and points at a hill and says, to nobody, "There is water under that." There is.

choices.text: Let {him} go, for now, and lick the fold of your tail

effects.log: It aches like a broken claw. The old rules said this would happen; the old rules are tiresome when they are right. You will find {npc} again. A human with your light inside cannot hide from you for long. (-4 health)

choices.text: Call {his} name after {him} down the road

effects.log: {npc} stops at the bottom of the hill, and turns, and looks up at you. For a moment there is your own light in {his} eyes. Then {he} runs again, faster. {He} knows now that you know. That will make it easier, or harder.

events.text: You find {npc} in a market town, living in a rented room, frightened of everything. {He} has not slept. {He} knows where every well in the town is, and every grave, and which houses are built on bad ground, and cannot stop knowing it. When you come to the door in a borrowed face {he} looks at you and goes grey. "I know your shadow," {he} says. "Take it back. Please. I did not want it."

choices.text: Hold out your hand and let {him} give it on a breath, freely

effects.log: It comes back on {his} breath, warm and frightened, and the folded tail opens like a fan. {npc} sits down on the floor and weeps with relief. "It was so loud," {he} says. "The whole earth, all the time." You know. You have heard it for centuries.

choices.text: Tell {him} to keep it, and learn to live with it

effects.log: "It will get quieter," you say. "You will become the best geomancer in three provinces." {npc} stares. You go back to the mound and begin, from a rice grain of light, to grow a new bead. The fold eases. It will take a century.

events.text: {npc} has become famous. A geomancer whose sites never fail: families wait a year for {him} to walk their hills. {He} has a fine robe and a fine compass, and does not need the compass. When you come to {his} gate in a borrowed face, {he} sends the servants away and receives you alone, and does not pretend.

choices.text: Ask for it back, honestly, as a debt

ok.log: A long night of talk. {npc} tells you what the earth sounds like; you tell {him} what it cost you. At dawn {he} gives it back on a breath, freely, and is an ordinary person again, with a fine robe and a compass {he} will now need. {He} says it is a relief. You almost believe {him}.

fail.log: "No," {npc} says, very politely. "I have a name now. I have a house. You will understand." You do understand. That is the trouble. You go away with the fold aching. (-5 health)

choices.text: Take it back the old way

effects.npcDie: a sudden fever the physicians could not name
effects.log: You take it back the old way, which the stories name and this one will not. The bead is yours again before dawn, and the tail opens. A month later there is a famous funeral, and the geomancer's family cannot understand why a fox sits on the hill above it every night.

choices.text: Let {him} keep it; the earth suits {him}

effects.log: "Keep it," you say. "Choose good graves. Choose them for the poor as well." {npc} promises, and keeps the promise, and you go home and start a new bead from nothing. The fold eases as the new light grows.

events.text: {npc} did not look at the earth when {he} fell. {He} looked at the people who came running, and now {he} sees people: what ails them, what they hide, how long they have. {He} keeps a physician's room in a poor quarter and is never wrong. When you come in, {he} looks at you and says, "Ah. You are very old, and you are missing something."

choices.text: Ask {him} to give it back

effects.log: {npc} thinks about the waiting room full of the poor, and then gives it back on a breath, freely, because it was yours. The next morning {he} is an ordinary physician with good habits. {He} stays in the poor quarter anyway. That part, it turns out, was {his}.

choices.text: Sit in the waiting room for a season and watch what {he} does with it

effects.log: A season of it: the coughs, the fevers, the children, the old. At the end you get up and leave without asking. A new grain of light begins in your mouth on the walk home, and the fold begins, slowly, to ease.

events.text: {npc} is very old: the geomancer, or the physician, whom your light made. {He} sends a servant up the hill road with a message for the fox of the grave mound, as if that were a perfectly ordinary address. The message says: come before the first snow. I want to give something back.

choices.text: Go, in your own shape

effects.log: {npc} is propped on cushions by an open door. You come in through the yard, a fox with all your tails, and the servants scatter. {He} laughs. On {his} last breath something warm passes to you across the room: not the bead, but what {he} learned with it. Then {he} is gone.

choices.text: Go in a borrowed face, and sit with {him} as a friend

effects.log: You sit by the bed and talk about hills and wells and graves, and the people who lie in them. {npc} says it was a good life, and a loud one. "Thank you for not taking it back," {he} says. {He} dies before the snow.

events.text: {npc}, who swallowed your bead once and gave it back, comes up the hill road many years later, grey, with a grandchild by the hand. {He} sits down on the mound without asking and says to the grandchild: "Never play games with strangers on this road." Then, to the grass: "I never told anyone. I wanted you to know that."

choices.text: Come out and sit with them both

effects.log: The grandchild is not afraid of you at all, which says something about how {npc} told the story at home. You sit together till dusk. When they go, {npc} bows to the mound as to a relative.

choices.text: Stay in the earth, and let them have their quiet

effects.log: They sit an hour and go. On the grass where they sat, {npc} has left a small thing: a smooth white river stone, the size of a bead. You keep it in the earth under the mound for a hundred years.

events.text: A salt peddler on the hill road at dusk, young, with an A-frame of salt sacks on his back and a forked stick in his hand that is far too old for him: the wood black with handling, the fork worn smooth. He stops when he sees your borrowed face coming the other way, and grips the stick, and does not lift it. He is shaking.

choices.text: Stop at a polite distance and wish him good evening

effects.log: "Good evening," {npc} says, after a while, in a voice that cracks. Neither of you moves. Then {he} steps off the road into the grass to let you by, which no salt peddler has done for a fox in the history of the world.

choices.text: Ask him whose stick that is

effects.log: "My grandfather's," {npc} says. "Grandfather said it would know you. It does. It is pulling at my hand like a dog on a rope." {He} holds it down with both hands. "I do not want to hit you," {he} says. "I want to know why Grandfather did."

choices.text: Go round him through the fields, the long way, as the old rule says

effects.log: Never cross a salt peddler. You cross the paddies instead, wet to the knee. When you look back from the far dyke, the young peddler is still standing in the road watching you, the stick lowered, as if waiting for something.

events.text: {npc} the salt peddler comes back up the hill road the next market day, and the next, and sits on the verge by your grave mound to eat {his} rice ball, with the old stick across {his} knees. "Grandfather caught a fox with this," {he} says to the mound. "An old one, in a hat. Never said why. Only that it was what salt peddlers are for."

choices.text: Come out and tell {him} the story from the fox's side

effects.log: The old fox in the hat that was not a hat, coming down to the village for a reason no fox ever told you; the courtesy of the villagers; the one man on the road who was not fooled. {npc} listens with the rice ball forgotten. "So Grandfather was right," {he} says. "And it was still sad." Yes.

choices.text: Tell {him} from the earth that some foxes need the stick, and some do not

effects.log: A voice from the grave mound. {npc} drops the rice ball. Then {he} picks it up, and dusts it, and says, "How do I know which?" You have no good answer. "Look at what they do," you say. "Not what they are." {He} thinks that is too easy. It is.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let {him} eat in peace

effects.log: {npc} eats, and talks to the mound about salt prices and a cousin's wedding, and goes on down the road. It becomes a habit, every market day for years. You come to look forward to the salt prices.

events.text: The fox hunters of the county come to {npc}'s salt store, because everyone knows the salt peddlers can see foxes. They want {him} to walk the hill road with them at dusk and point. There is a bounty. {He} has a family now, and the salt trade is bad this year.

choices.text: Let {him} choose, and do not interfere

ok.log: {npc} walks the hill road with the hunters at dusk and points at every bush but the one by your mound. They go home empty. The next market day {he} sits by the mound and says, "I told them the stick was broken." It is not.

fail.log: {npc} points. Not at you: at the hill. It is enough. Three nights of dogs. You get away with a torn ear, and the next market day the rice ball on the verge is left uneaten, and {npc} does not come for a year. (-10 health)

choices.text: Leave a sack of good salt-fish on {his} step, so {he} can say no

effects.log: Enough to see the family through the bad year. {npc} says no to the hunters. {He} never asks where the fish came from. {He} salts it very well.

choices.text: Move to the far hill for a season

effects.log: You spare {npc} the choice by not being there. When you come back the hunters have gone to another county. {He} is sitting on the verge with the stick. "I would have said no," {he} says. Maybe.

events.text: {npc} is old, and gives up the salt road. On the last day {he} comes up the hill with the forked stick wrapped in a cloth and lays it on the grass of your mound. "My grandson is not a salt peddler," {he} says. "Nobody will need this. I thought it should go where it was always going."

choices.text: Take it into the earth and keep it
