effects.log: A fox sleeping beside the stick made to catch it. The wood is warm from all those hands. {npc} dies that winter, and the stick stays with you in the dark under the mound for the rest of your long life.

choices.text: Tell {him} to burn it, so no child of {his} line ever has to choose

effects.log: You burn it together on the mound at dusk, an old peddler and an old fox, and watch the fork go last. {npc} dies that winter. The smell of the smoke stays in the grass till spring.

events.text: You have led drunks home and bandits astray on these hills for centuries, and now three villages have begun to pray to you. There is a little shrine on the ridge, old and weathered, and they have started leaving rice and candles there for the light that walks the hill roads at night. Last night a woman left a pair of baby shoes on the step, and asked for a child.

choices.text: Take the offerings, and answer some of the prayers

effects.log: A lost goat found, a sick ox cured, a fever broken. The villages say the shrine on the ridge has woken up. They bring more rice, and more candles, and the bead in your mouth warms at every prayer, the way it warms at a borrowed breath. That should worry you more than it does.

choices.text: Leave the offerings where they lie

effects.log: The rice goes to the birds and the candles burn down. The villages decide the shrine is asleep again. Only the woman with the baby shoes keeps coming, and you find you cannot stop watching her climb.

choices.text: Go down in a borrowed face and become the shrine's keeper

effects.log: A keeper in a white jacket who sweeps the step and lights the candles and says the goddess hears everything. The villages are delighted. Your borrowed face is prayed past every day. It is the strangest mask you have ever worn.

events.text: An old woman in a faded jacket sits on the step of the shrine at noon, where the offerings are, and does not eat them. She looks at you with eyes the colour of the mountain in winter. "That is my shrine," she says. "I have kept this mountain since before your grandmother's grandmother was a kit. They pray to you now. Where am I to go?"

choices.text: Give it back to her, and tell the villages they were wrong

effects.log: You stand on the step in the rain and tell three villages they have been praying to a fox. Some believe you. Most are angry, at you, or at the fox, or at being fools. The old woman goes back into her shrine without a word, and the next morning the candles are lit by nobody.

choices.text: Keep it. A mountain belongs to whoever the people pray to

effects.log: "Then you will learn what a mountain costs," the old woman says, and gets up stiffly, and walks away down the far side of the ridge. The sky over the mountain stays very clear, and very watchful, all summer.

choices.text: Offer to share it: the villages pray, and she answers

effects.log: She considers you a long time. "A fox as my doorkeeper," she says. "It has been done before. Badly." But she sits down again on the step, and that night the offerings are gone in the morning, and so is some of the warmth in your bead.

events.text: Three strangers come up the ridge in a squall, tall and dripping, in blue-green robes with pearls at their collars, and the stream beside the path runs backwards as they pass. The Dragon King's three brothers, come from the deep pool below the mountain to see who rules here now. "Not the old woman," the eldest says, looking at you. "A fox. Our brother will want to know."

choices.text: Call down blades of fire and fight them for the mountain

ok.log: Paper flies up from the shrine and catches fire in the air, and the fire is blades. The three brothers go back down to their pool, cut and steaming, faster than they came. The villages see the fire on the ridge and pray harder than ever. Far below, in the deep water, somebody begins a letter to heaven.

fail.log: Fire against water, three against one. They put your blades out in the squall and throw you down the ridge into the stream. "Tell the old woman to come back," the eldest says, "or our brother will tell heaven." (-15 health)

choices.text: Bow, and tell them the mountain is the old woman's

effects.log: The eldest looks at you with long cold eyes. "A fox that bows," he says. "My brother will not believe it." They go down to the pool. The stream runs forwards again.

choices.text: Lead them round the ridge in the rain till dawn

effects.log: Foxfire in the squall. Three dragon princes walk round the same ridge all night, getting wetter, which is a strange thing to do to dragons. At dawn they go home furious and laughing at each other. They will remember you.

events.text: The old woman of the mountain did not go far. You find her living in a charcoal-burner's hut in the next valley, teaching the charcoal-burner's children the names of every plant on the slope. When she sees you at the door she goes on with the lesson, and only at the end says, "Well? Have you come to learn, or to gloat?"

choices.text: To learn

effects.log: A season of it: where the springs rise, which slopes slide, how a mountain feels a fire coming. "You will need this one day," she says, "if you ever become what you are pretending to be." You do not ask which thing she means.

choices.text: To ask what heaven will do

effects.log: "Wind," she says. "Rain. Lightning. Three of them, always three. They will not come for you while the villages love you. They will come when the villages love you too much." She goes back to the children.

events.text: The sky gathers over the mountain. Three clouds, one from the east with a wind in it, one from the south heavy with rain, one from the north with a light inside like a lamp behind paper. They stop over the ridge and wait. Down in the villages, the people are praying to you to stop the storm, which is the one thing you cannot do.

choices.text: Go down to the charcoal-burner's hut, and bring the old woman home

effects.log: You walk her up the ridge yourself through the first gusts, her hand on your shoulder. At the shrine she sits down on the step, and the three clouds hang there a long moment, and then go back the way they came. The villages are confused for a generation. The mountain is not.

choices.text: Run, and let the mountain sort itself out

effects.log: You go down the far side of the ridge at a dead run with the lightning walking behind you, one strike for every hundred paces. It stops at the river. The shrine is empty when the villages come; then, in a week, it is not, and nobody can say who lit the candles.

choices.text: Climb onto the shrine roof and face them

effects.log: You stand on the roof of the stolen shrine with all your tails spread and the paper flying up round you into blades of fire. The wind comes first, then the rain, then the light. When the villages climb the ridge in the morning there is only the old woman sweeping the step, and the candles relit, and on the grass a scorched shape that they bury without asking what it was.

events.text: The woman who left the baby shoes on the shrine step comes up the ridge again with a small child on her back. She sets the child down before the shrine and makes it bow, and bows herself, and leaves a bowl of the first rice of the year. The child looks past the shrine straight at the bush where you are lying.

choices.text: Let the child see you, just for a moment

effects.log: The child points and opens its mouth, and the mother turns, and there is only a bush. "A fox," says the child. "A fox with lots of tails." The mother smiles and says, "That is the goddess," and the child, who knows better, says nothing.

choices.text: Stay hidden, and leave the rice for the old woman

effects.log: You do not touch the bowl. In the morning it is empty anyway, and a single grey hair lies across it, long and fine. The old woman of the mountain has her own ways of saying thank you.

events.text: The lamp. You forgot the lamp. {npc} comes in with it to ask you something ordinary, and stops in the doorway, and the light goes past you onto the paper wall, and there it is: your shadow, with all your tails in it, laid out across the wall like a fan. {npc} does not scream. That is the worst part. {He} only says your borrowed name, once, as a question.

choices.text: Run: the window, the yard, the hill

effects.log: Out through the paper of the window and over the wall before {npc} has finished the breath. Behind you the scream comes at last, and then the dogs, and then the whole lane. You do not stop until the grave mounds, and you do not look back.

choices.text: Answer {him}: say sorry, in your own voice, and then go

effects.log: "I am sorry," you say, and it comes out in the voice under the borrowed one, the voice from the earth under the mound. {npc} sets the lamp down very carefully on the floor. You go out of the door, not the window. Nobody follows you for a whole hour.

choices.text: Turn over three times and be gone before the shadow is believed

effects.log: Three turns in the air and there is nothing in the room but a dropped cushion and a smell of pine. {npc} will spend years deciding whether {he} saw it. The village will not; the village decides that same night.

events.text: A lamp in the palace corridor, held by {npc}, who has walked this corridor beside you every night for years. Your shadow on the paper screen has too many tails, and {npc} sees them, and the lamp shakes. Somewhere a door slides. A guard calls out. By morning the court will be calling for dogs.

choices.text: Go over the wall before the first dog is loosed

effects.log: Roofs, a gate tower, the moat, the hills. By dawn the palace is full of yellow dogs and you are three ridges away. The court will write it down: a fox in the palace. They always do.

choices.text: Ask {npc}, quietly, to lower the lamp

ok.log: {npc} lowers it. The shadow shrinks to a person. "Go," {he} whispers, "out by the kitchen court." You go. At the morning council {npc} swears there was nothing in the corridor but a cat, and is believed, because {he} has never lied before.

fail.log: {npc} screams. The guards come at a run, and one of them has a spear and is quick. You go out through the screen with the spear in your flank, and over the wall with it, and pull it out in a ditch at dawn. (-8 health)

choices.text: Stand still, and let them see what served them

effects.log: You turn to face the corridor with all your tails in the light. The guards stop. The ministers in their night robes stop. For one long breath the whole palace looks at what has been taking its pulse and copying its letters. Then you walk out, slowly, and nobody stops you.

events.text: {npc} comes up to the shrine at dawn with an offering and finds the keeper asleep on the step in the first sun, and the keeper's shadow has tails. {npc} drops the rice. By noon three villages know that they have been praying to a fox.

choices.text: Leave the mountain before they come

effects.log: You go over the ridge before the first torches. Behind you the villages burn the offerings and then, not knowing what else to do, light the candles again for whoever is really there. The old woman of the mountain, perhaps.

choices.text: Stay, and tell them the truth to their faces

effects.log: They come up with sticks and you are sitting on the step in your own shape. "I found the goats," you say. "I broke the fevers. I am a fox. All of that is true." They do not know what to do with it. In the end they go home, and some of them still leave rice.

events.text: A lamp carried past a paper door at the wrong moment; a shadow on the paper with tails in it; a scream. Then dogs, from every yard in the lane at once, and torches, and somebody shouting for the salt peddler. The face you have worn for years falls off you like a wet sheet.

choices.text: Run for the hills by the paddy dykes

effects.log: The dykes, the stream, the reed beds. The old way out, the one you learned as a field fox with the hunting dogs behind you. It still works. It always will. That is the only comfort in it.

choices.text: Lead the torches round the marsh till they tire

effects.log: Foxfire in the reeds. Half the village follows the wrong lights all night and comes home soaked and quarrelling. The other half sits up with the doors barred. By morning, the person they knew is only a story.

choices.text: Go back for one thing you cannot leave

ok.log: In through the back while the lane is full of torches, and out again with it: a cup, a letter, a child's drawing of the keeper of the house. It is not worth what you risked. It is worth more than anything else you own.

fail.log: A dog meets you in the back room. You get out with the thing in your teeth and the dog's teeth in your leg. (-12 health)

events.text: It is {npc}'s child who sees it, of all people: woken in the night, padding out for water, looking up at the paper door with the lamp behind it. Tail after tail, the child counts them out loud, carefully, the way you taught them to count. Then the child calls for {npc}.

choices.text: Put a finger to your lips, and go before {npc} comes

effects.log: The child nods solemnly and keeps the secret for nearly a whole minute. By then you are on the hill. Behind you {npc} is holding the child and staring at the empty door, and the dogs are beginning.

choices.text: Wait for {npc}, and let the child see you go in your own shape

effects.log: {npc} comes out with a lamp and sees you whole, all your tails, standing in the yard. You bow to {him}, once, as a guest bows leaving a house. Then the hill. The child grows up to tell it as the best night of a whole childhood.

events.text: Years after the night the face fell. You pass the old house at dusk, in a different shape, and see that {npc} still keeps a cup at the end of the table, the place where you used to sit, and fills it at New Year, and talks to it. Nobody else in the house knows why.

choices.text: Go in, in your own shape, and sit in your place

effects.log: {npc} looks up and goes white, and then pours the cup full and pushes it across. Neither of you says anything for a long time. Then {npc} begins to tell you about the neighbours, as if it were any evening at all.

choices.text: Leave something at the gate: a hare, a bundle of herbs

effects.log: In the morning {npc} finds it and stands at the gate a long time, looking up at the hill. That evening the cup is filled again, with the good wine this time.

choices.text: Walk on. It is better for {him} without you

effects.log: You walk on up the hill road. Maybe it is better. You will never know, and that is the price, and you paid it the night you forgot the lamp.

events.text: The village has not forgotten. The headman has hired hunters with dogs, and a salt peddler to walk in front of them, and they are coming up the hill to the grave mounds at noon, when a fox sleeps, beating the long grass.

choices.text: Stand and face the dogs at the mound

ok.log: The dogs come over the mound and meet something they do not have a word for, and go back down the hill faster than they came, and the hunters with them. The salt peddler stays a moment longer, looking at you, and then follows.

fail.log: Too many dogs. You go out of the back of the earth and down the stream with blood in the water behind you. They dig out the earth under the mound and find nothing but old bedding. (-18 health)

choices.text: Go to ground in another earth till the summer is over

effects.log: A badger's old sett on the far hill, damp and smelly and safe. You lie in it all summer and listen to the dogs on the wrong hill. By autumn the headman has spent his money and the hunters have gone home.

choices.text: Lead them in circles round the graves

effects.log: A tail seen here, a bark there, foxfire in broad noon among the mounds. By dusk every dog is hoarse and every hunter swears the graveyard is haunted, which, in a way, it is. They do not come back.

events.text: You hear {npc} telling it in the market, years later, to a ring of children: the keeper with the tails, the lamp, the night. {He} tells it well. {He} gets the number of tails right. And {he} ends it the way nobody else in the village ends it: "And it never once hurt anybody in that house. Remember that part."

choices.text: Let the story be told, and go

effects.log: You go on through the market in a stranger's face. Behind you the children are arguing about whether a fox can be good. It is the best thing anyone has ever said about you, and you heard it by accident.

choices.text: Stop at the edge of the ring and correct one detail

effects.log: "It was the left-hand lamp," you say, "not the right." {npc} looks up at you and goes very still. Then {he} says, "The left-hand lamp," to the children, and goes on, and does not look at you again until you are gone.

events.text: A full moon over the rock cave where you have taken to sleeping, below a hermitage on a cliff. A voice comes out of the sky, not loud, not unkind, the way a teacher speaks to a slow student: "One human, freely, writes you a poem, and you may be born human. Not taken. Not tricked. Given." Then the moon is only the moon again.

choices.text: Bow to the sky, and begin to wait

effects.log: You bow until your nose touches the stone. A poem. You have heard ten thousand poems in your masks, written for kings and wine-houses and dead wives. Not one of them for you. You decide you can wait.

choices.text: Ask the sky: what kind of poem?

effects.log: No answer. Of course no answer. The sky does not repeat itself for foxes. You lie awake all night composing, in your head, the poem you would want, and it is very bad, and that is a kind of answer too.

choices.text: Laugh: who would write a fox a poem?

effects.log: Your laugh echoes round the cave. Nobody would. That is the point, you suppose. Heaven does not set easy tests. You go to sleep annoyed, and wake up hoping.

events.text: Years of waiting. In every mask you have asked for poems: at the wine-house, at the herb stall, from scholars who drank too much and owed you. They wrote you poems about wine, about the moon, about the keeper's lovely eyes. Not one of them was for a fox, because not one of them knew there was a fox to write for.

choices.text: Keep waiting, honestly

effects.log: You put the poems away in a box in the cave, all of them, even the bad ones. A poem freely given to a mask is still a poem. It is just not the right one. You keep the box.

choices.text: Tell one scholar the truth, and ask

effects.log: The scholar laughs, then stops laughing, then runs. The next morning there is a poem nailed to your door: it is about foxes, and it is not kind. It is honest, though. You keep that one too.

choices.text: Think about whether a tricked poem would count

effects.log: You could. You could get a poem out of anyone: a borrowed face, a sad story, a breath. You sit with that for a long time. "Not taken," the voice said. "Not tricked." You decide the sky meant it.

events.text: In a later year of waiting you are a guest, in a borrowed face, at the house of an official named Kang. {npc}, the youngest of the house, sleeps in the next room, and {his} breath is warm and bright as sunlight on water. Years of waiting have made the bead very dim. A thread, you think. Only one.

choices.text: Take the thread

effects.log: One thread, in the dark. In the morning {npc} is pale and cannot rise, and the house sends for physicians, and then for an exorcist, and then for the son of a famous man who is said to bind spirits. You knew this was how the old story went. You did it anyway.

choices.text: Leave the house that night, before you do

effects.log: You thank your host at dinner and are gone by the second watch, with your sandals in your hand. Kang thinks you rude. {npc} wakes in the morning rosy and cross and never knows how close it was.

choices.text: Lend the bead instead: {npc} has a cough

effects.log: The other way round: your bead to {npc}, for a night, on your breath. The cough goes. The bead comes back dimmer still. You go back to the cave to wait, poorer and lighter.

events.text: {npc}, the son of a famous man, comes to the rock cave with cords of red thread and a bundle of talismans, and {he} is good at it: the cords go round the cave mouth before you are awake, and you wake bound. {He} sits down outside on a stone with a sword across {his} knees and says, "Before I do anything: tell me why."

choices.text: Fight the cords and {him}

ok.log: The red cords burn and part. You go past {npc} in a rush of tails and are on the ridge before {he} is on {his} feet. {He} does not follow. {He} sits back down on the stone and, after a while, you see {him} begin to write something.

fail.log: The cords hold. You throw yourself against them until you bleed, and then lie still. {npc} waits, patient as a heron. "Now," {he} says. "Why?" (-15 health)

choices.text: Tell {him} everything: the voice, the waiting, the poem

effects.log: You tell it from the moon to now, and do not leave out the bad parts. {npc} listens without moving. When you finish {he} is quiet a long time, and then {he} says, "My father wrote poems."

choices.text: Lie to {him}: say you are a lost mountain spirit

effects.log: {npc} looks at you with {his} father's eyes. "You are a fox," {he} says gently, "and you are lying, and you are tired. Try again." You do. The second time, it is the truth.

events.text: {npc} unrolls a sheet of paper on the stone before the cave: a poem in {his} father's hand, old, about smoke and dark mist curling round a lonely grave, and a guest who will not stay. "My father wrote it for nobody," {npc} says. "I give it to you. Freely. I would rather you were a person who owes me than a fox I killed."

choices.text: Take it, and bow to the ground

effects.log: You take it in your teeth, very carefully, and lay it on the stone and bow until your forehead is on it. Nothing happens: no thunder, no voice. Then the red cords fall off the cave mouth on their own, and {npc} stands up and goes home without looking back.

choices.text: Unfold the other poem first, the one already in the den

effects.log: Folded in the earth under your first mound all these years: a poem a human once wrote you on a path nobody else could find. You lay it beside the father's poem. {npc} reads it, and reads it again, and says, "Then you did not need mine." You did. Two is better than one.

choices.text: Unfold the honest poem from the den, the one that knew what you had done

effects.log: A poem from a human who asked what you did while you waited, and heard all of it, and wrote anyway. It is not flattering. {npc} reads it and laughs aloud for the first time. "That one is better than my father's," {he} says. "Do not tell anyone."

choices.text: Refuse it: you have hurt this house

effects.log: "Not from you," you say. "Not after Kang's house." {npc} rolls the poem up again and sits a while. "Then you will wait longer," {he} says. "Good." {He} cuts the cords and goes. You do wait longer. It is the right kind of waiting.

events.text: Nothing happens. You are still a fox. The poem lies in the cave in a box with the others, and on clear nights you take it out and read it by the light of the bead. It is a door, you begin to understand, not a road. The thousand days are the road, and the hundred unseen. The poem only tells you the door is there.

choices.text: Keep the poem, and keep walking

effects.log: You fold it into the box and go out into the morning. A door you can see is a great deal better than a door you have to imagine.

choices.text: Write a poem back, for the one who held the cords

effects.log: It takes you a whole winter. It is about a man who sat on a stone with a sword across his knees and did not use it. You leave it at his gate. Years later you hear that he had it carved on his father's grave.

events.text: A new governor has come to the province from the capital, and he feels the cold. He has seen a white fox collar on a minister's winter robe and wants one. The bounty is posted at every market cross: a year's rice for a white fox, and twice that for the fox of the grave mounds, which the villages say is silver in the moonlight.

choices.text: Laugh: you are red, not white

effects.log: You are red. In the moonlight, on the mound, with the bead bright, perhaps not so red. The hunters of three counties are already oiling their traps. They do not care what colour you are by day.

choices.text: Go and read the bounty notice in a borrowed face

effects.log: The governor's seal, the governor's price, the governor's cold. A hunter beside you reads it aloud for the others and spits. "Silver in the moonlight," he says. "I know that hill." He does.

choices.text: Move to the far mountains until the governor leaves

effects.log: Governors stay three years. You go north into the high pines and wait. The hunters search your hill all winter and find an empty earth. But the bounty stays up, and governors, it turns out, sometimes stay longer.

events.text: The first snow, and the hunting party with it: twenty men in fur hats, dogs on leashes, a falcon on a glove, and at the front {npc}, a young hunter who reads tracks the way a scholar reads characters. {He} kneels at the edge of your hill and touches the snow, and looks straight up at the bush where you are lying.

choices.text: Break away across the open snow before the dogs are loosed

ok.log: Over the ridge, down the frozen stream, through a village and out the other side with half its dogs behind you. You lose them all by dusk. {npc} does not chase. {He} stands at the top of the hill watching which way you went, and remembers.

fail.log: The falcon comes down on you in the open. You shake it off and lose an ear-tip and a handful of fur, and get away bleeding into the pines. The fur is red. {npc} picks it up from the snow and puts it in {his} sleeve. (-16 health)

choices.text: Hide the tails and lie still till they pass

effects.log: You make yourself a fox-shaped drift of snow and breathe once an hour. The party goes by, dogs and all. Only {npc} stops, and looks at the drift, and says something very quietly to the snow. Then {he} walks on.

choices.text: Lead them up the wrong valley with foxfire on the snow

effects.log: Lights on the snow at dusk, always a valley ahead. The party goes after them till midnight. {npc} does not. {He} sits by the hill with {his} hands in {his} sleeves until the others come back cold and furious, and says, "It was never up there."

events.text: A trap at the foot of your hill, set with a scent you would know anywhere: White-Paw's, or White-Paw's kin. In a wicker cage behind the snare, a young vixen with two white forepaws is crying, very quietly, as foxes cry when they have already cried a great deal. The snare is set for whatever comes to her.

choices.text: Go to her, and spring the snare with a stick first

ok.log: The snare snaps on the stick. You chew the wicker open and she is out and gone into the pines like a struck spark, not looking back. She has White-Paw's run. You sit by the empty cage a while longer than is wise.

fail.log: There was a second snare. It takes your hind leg and you are three hours chewing out of it, and the vixen is free and gone long before you are. You limp home as the dogs begin. (-15 health)

choices.text: Leave her; it is what the trap wants

effects.log: You go round. Behind you the crying stops in the night, and you do not go back to find out why. The governor's collar has nothing to do with it, you tell yourself. It is only snow and a trap.

choices.text: Come back in a borrowed face and buy the vixen from the trapper

effects.log: A traveller who wants a pet fox for a child. The trapper sells, puzzled. You walk her into the pines and open the basket. She looks at you, and at your shadow, and knows. Then she goes.

events.text: The governor himself is ill: a chill in the lungs that has kept him in bed since the second snow, wrapped in every fur in the province except the one he wants. His physicians are frightened. The bounty is doubled again, as if a white collar would cure him.

choices.text: Go to him as a physician, cure him, and ask him to take the bounty down

effects.log: A night with the bead, a morning with warm ginger. He sits up by noon. You ask your fee: the bounty taken down. He laughs, and pays it, and the notices come off the market crosses. He never knows what he paid to.

choices.text: Let the chill take its course

effects.log: The chill takes its course. He lives, barely, and goes back to the capital in the spring wrapped in ordinary sheepskin, and the next governor does not care about foxes. You did nothing. Sometimes that is enough. You are not proud of it.

choices.text: Visit his sickroom at night, in your own shape, and sit on the end of his bed

effects.log: He wakes and sees you: all your tails, the bead lit, sitting on his winter furs. He does not scream. He is too ill. In the morning the bounty is taken down, and the governor never speaks of foxes again, nor wears a fur collar.

events.text: The last hunt of the winter: the hunters of three counties together, sixty men and every dog they own, and {npc} at the head of them, who has learned you over the winters the way a scholar learns a book. They have you on a bare ridge in deep snow at dusk, and every way down has a line of torches.

choices.text: Run the knife-edge of the ridge where no dog can follow

ok.log: Along the rock where the snow overhangs the drop, one paw wide. The dogs stop. The men stop. {npc} does not stop until the very edge, and then {he} stops too, and watches you go along the sky with your tails lit, and lowers {his} bow.

fail.log: The snow gives way under you. You fall a long way into a drift, and lie broken in it for a day, and crawl out at night when the hunters have gone home sure you are dead under it. (-15 health)

choices.text: Walk down to {npc} and look {him} in the eye

effects.log: You come down the slope slowly, straight to {npc}, and sit in the snow in front of {him}. {He} has the bow drawn. {He} looks at you a long, long time. Then {he} turns to the sixty men and says, loudly, "That is not the one." And they go home.

choices.text: Lie down in the snow and let it end

effects.log: You lie down in the snow with your tails round you and let {npc} come. {He} is quick, and kind about it, as good hunters are. That winter a governor wears a collar of fur that looks silver in the lamplight, and in later lives men pay fortunes for it and do not sleep well.

events.text: A grey fox from the next county comes to your mound, thin and bright-eyed, with a bead in its mouth like a small hot coal. You have heard of it: the fox who counts. "Ninety-eight," it says. "Students, all asleep, all pale in the morning, none of them dead. Two more and I go up to heaven, the old way. The rule says I need a witness. Come and watch."

choices.text: Go with it, to watch, and decide there

effects.log: You go. It talks the whole way: which village schools sleep sound, which masters keep dogs, which students breathe deepest. It is not cruel. It is something worse: it is very, very patient.

choices.text: Refuse, and ask what the hundredth student will be like

effects.log: "The hundredth always wakes," it says. "I know. I have a plan." Every fox who ever counted had a plan. You do not say so. It goes off down the hill alone, counting under its breath.

choices.text: Go ahead of it to the school, and warn the master

effects.log: A stranger at the schoolmaster's gate at dusk, saying strange things about foxes. The old master listens, nods, and says he has heard the story. "Swallow it and look at the sky," he says. "I tell them every year." He does not look surprised by you at all.

events.text: The ninety-ninth: a sleeping student at a village school, pale already from a cold, and the grey fox at the open paper door with the bead glowing. It looks back at you, its witness, and goes in. You hear the thread drawn, thin as silk. Ninety-nine. Then it looks along the row of sleepers for the hundredth, and chooses {npc}.

choices.text: Wake {npc} before the fox reaches {him}

effects.log: A pebble against the shutter. {npc} sits up, blinking, and looks straight at the grey fox in the room, and remembers every word the schoolmaster ever said. The fox freezes. So, in the doorway, do you.

choices.text: Witness, as you promised, and say nothing

effects.log: You stand in the doorway and watch. You do not stop it. The grey fox kneels beside {npc} and the bead goes down toward the sleeper's breath. And {npc} opens {his} eyes.

choices.text: Stop the grey fox at the door

ok.log: Tails against tails in the dark yard, quick and silent. It goes over the wall with ninety-nine and no more, cursing you in the old fox tongue. The students sleep through it all. {npc} wakes up in the morning with a strange dream about two foxes and a lamp.

fail.log: It is older than it looks, and desperate. It throws you across the yard into the woodpile and goes back in. And {npc}, woken by the crash, opens {his} eyes and sees it bending over {him}. (-14 health)

events.text: The hundredth wakes, as the hundredth always does. {npc} sits up with the grey fox's bead half in {his} breath, and the old schoolmaster's words in {his} head, and swallows. Then {he} is up and out of the door and running, and falls in the yard, and lies there with {his} face to the earth. The grey fox stands in the doorway like a thing made of ash.

choices.text: Lead the grey fox away before the school wakes

effects.log: It follows you like a sleepwalker, over the wall, up the hill. At the top it sits down and says, in an ordinary fox's voice, "Ninety-nine." That is all it says. It will never say anything else.

choices.text: Go to {npc} in the yard, and tell {him} what {he} is looking at

effects.log: "The earth," you say. "Wells, veins, the graves of the old. You will never see the sky. Nobody does." {npc} lifts {his} face out of the dirt and looks at you, and sees, you think, exactly what you are. "Thank you," {he} says. Then the school wakes.

choices.text: Watch, and remember what counting costs

effects.log: A hundred breaths, a hundred pale mornings, and it ends in a yard in the dark with the bead in somebody else. You will remember this every time your own bead is dim and a sleeper's breath is warm. That is what the witness was for.

events.text: Years later, on the road to that village school, you find the grey fox in a ditch: an ordinary fox now, old and thin and grey at the muzzle, lying in the long grass by the school wall, listening to the students recite the Thousand Character Classic inside. It does not know you. It is not unhappy. It is listening.

choices.text: Lie down beside it in the ditch for a while

effects.log: Heaven is dark, earth is yellow, the students chant. You lie in the grass beside the old fox until the lesson ends. It sleeps. You think about how close every fox is, every day, to this ditch.

choices.text: Bring it a hen from a careless yard

effects.log: It eats, and licks its paws, and looks at you without any idea who you are, and goes back to listening. A kindness to a stranger. It is the only kind you can do it now.

events.text: A dokkaebi turns up at your door at dusk with a club over its shoulder and a dish of buckwheat jelly as a present. It has seen your borrowed face at the market and admired it for a year. "The harvest feast," it says. "One night. They will not let me in looking like this. Lend me the face. I will bring it back. Probably."
events.arc: The Dokkaebi Who Wanted a Face

choices.text: Lend it, for one night only

effects.log: You take the face off like a hat, which is a very strange feeling, and fit it on the dokkaebi, which is stranger. It looks at itself in the water jar and is overcome. You spend the night under the porch with nothing on but your own fur.

choices.text: Lend it, if the dokkaebi will owe you a favour

effects.log: "A favour," it agrees, and spits on its hand, and shakes yours. A dokkaebi's favour is worth a great deal, if you can get it to remember. You take the face off and hand it over.

choices.text: Refuse: the face is yours, and it is fragile

effects.log: The dokkaebi is offended. It eats the buckwheat jelly itself on your step, loudly, and goes off into the dark grumbling. For a month afterwards your well water tastes faintly of buckwheat.

choices.text: Go with it: an old friend, lend it a spare face of the bead's making

effects.log: The same dokkaebi who thought you rude on the marsh, long ago. You make it a face of its own out of moonlight and bead, and go to the feast together, two strangers nobody can quite place. It is the best night out you have had in a century.

events.text: The harvest feast, from a rooftop. Your face is down there in the wrestling ring, and it is winning. It has thrown the miller, the blacksmith and two brothers from the next village, and is now eating the prize ox's share of buckwheat jelly with both hands. The whole village is cheering for the keeper of your house.
events.arc: The Dokkaebi Who Wanted a Face

choices.text: Let it have its night

effects.log: It wins the ox. It gives the ox away to a widow. It sings a song nobody knows and everybody joins. At dawn it comes back up the lane, very happy, very muddy, carrying your face slightly crooked.

choices.text: Go down and stop it before it wrestles the headman

effects.log: You cannot go down as yourself, so you go down as nobody in particular and whisper to it in the crowd. It is too late. It has already thrown the headman, very gently, into the pond. The village has never been so happy.

events.text: The dokkaebi brings your face back at dawn, and hands it over, and does not quite meet your eye. There is a dent in the forehead, round and deep, exactly the shape of the end of a club. "Somebody else had a club," it says. "I won. Mostly."
events.arc: The Dokkaebi Who Wanted a Face

choices.text: Put it on, dent and all

effects.log: The village is very impressed with the dent. You are now, it appears, a famous wrestler who took a blow from a dokkaebi's club and won the ox. People bring their sons to see you. The dent is permanent. So, now, is the reputation.

choices.text: Smooth the dent with the bead, at a cost

effects.log: A night of moonlight and patience. The dent goes. In the morning the village asks where your bruise went, and you tell them you heal quickly. They had already noticed that.

events.text: Years later, the dokkaebi comes back to pay its favour, which it has remembered, to its own great surprise. It brings nothing. "A favour," it says. "I watched you all night at the feast, from inside your face. You are very tired of being looked at. So: for one year, nobody will look at you twice."
events.arc: The Dokkaebi Who Wanted a Face

choices.text: Accept, gratefully

effects.log: A year of being invisible in plain sight. Dogs yawn at you. Salt peddlers walk past. Your own neighbours forget your name twice. It is the most restful year you have had since the earth under the mound.

choices.text: Ask it instead to look after the village school's roof

effects.log: It stares. Then it laughs so hard it drops the club. "A fox," it says, "asking for a roof." But the school roof never leaks again in a hundred years, and at the harvest feast a strange wrestler with a dented forehead sometimes turns up and wins the ox.

events.text: Your borrowed face must cross a mountain pass to reach the next province, and the pass is held. Travellers wait at the inn at the bottom in fifties, because the old tiger of the ridge, the one with the white tail, has been taking a toll this year: an ox, a pig, or a traveller, its choice. You go up anyway, alone, at dusk. Halfway up it is lying across the path.

choices.text: Walk up to it as a person, and ask to pass

effects.log: It looks at you with eyes like two lamps behind paper, and then it looks at your shadow, and then, unmistakably, it laughs. "A fox," it says, in a voice like stones grinding, "in a pedlar's jacket. Sit down. Nobody interesting has come up this pass in years."

choices.text: Drop the face and meet it as what you are

effects.log: Your tails on the stones of the path. The tiger lifts its head and sniffs, and lays its ears back, and then forward. "Better," it says. "I do not talk to masks. Sit."

choices.text: Go round by the goat path above, in the dark

ok.log: Over the shoulder of the ridge on goat-tracks, and down the far side at dawn. Behind you, the tiger yawns. It knew. It let you. You are not sure whether to be grateful or insulted.

fail.log: A stone turns under you and you come down the scree in a slide, right at the tiger's feet. It looks at you. "Sit down," it says. "Before you hurt yourself." (-12 health)

events.text: The tiger of the pass wants a bargain. "There is a pedlar," it says, "who comes up this pass every spring and sells the villages on the other side rotten salt and false ginseng. I would eat him, but the mountain god has told me to stop eating pedlars. You are good at being people. Do something about him. Then you may cross whenever you like."

choices.text: Agree, and make the pedlar honest the fox's way

effects.log: A season of foxfire on his road, his false ginseng turning into real roots overnight, his rotten salt into good salt, until he is so frightened of his own pack that he sells only what is true. The tiger is delighted. "Better than eating him," it admits. "Slower, but better."

choices.text: Agree, and simply follow the pedlar and tell every village

effects.log: A travelling stranger who arrives in each village a day before the pedlar, with samples. By the end of spring he cannot sell a grain. He takes up farming. The tiger thinks this is the funniest thing it has heard in a century.

choices.text: Refuse: you do not do a tiger's errands

effects.log: The tiger shrugs, as much as a tiger can. "Then pay the toll like anyone," it says, and you give it a whole season of hares, and it lets you over. Pride is expensive on a mountain.

events.text: Rain from a clear sky on the pass, the sun shining straight through it, every pine dripping light. The tiger lifts its head and sniffs the air and looks, for a moment, very young. "Fox rain," it says. "A tiger is marrying somewhere. I was a cub on a ridge in the mist the first time I saw it, and a little red fox in a hedge looked straight back at me."

choices.text: Tell it: that was me

effects.log: It stares at you through the shining rain for a long time. Then it puts its great head down and pushes it, once, against your shoulder, like a cat. "I knew it," it says. "I knew there was a reason I did not eat you."

choices.text: Sit with it in the shining rain until it stops

effects.log: Two old beasts on a wet pass with the sun on them. The rain stops. The tiger says nothing else about weddings, or hedges, or cubs, and neither do you, and that is how you become friends.

choices.text: Say that foxes and tigers both marry in the rain, in the stories

effects.log: The tiger snorts. "Stories," it says. "Humans will marry anything to anything in a story." But it looks pleased, and when you go down the pass it walks beside you all the way to the treeline.

events.text: Soldiers come up the pass with nets and spears and a captain who has a commission from the governor to rid the road of the tiger. They stop at your wine-house, or your stall, or wherever your borrowed face is this year, and ask the way to its den. You know the way. They know you know: the whole valley says the keeper is friends with something on the mountain.

choices.text: Send them up the wrong valley with a straight face

effects.log: You draw them a beautiful map. They spend a month on the wrong mountain. When they come back down they are thin and furious and the captain never quite proves anything. The tiger sends you a deer, in the night, left on the step.

choices.text: Go up first in the night and warn the tiger

effects.log: A fox at the den mouth at midnight, saying soldiers. The tiger yawns and moves to the next ridge. "You owe me nothing," it says. You know. It is not about owing.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: the tiger stopped eating travellers years ago

effects.log: The captain does not believe you, then half believes you, then asks the inn. The inn agrees. The soldiers go home with a report that says the tiger is reformed, which is the strangest report the governor ever reads.

events.text: The fifth tail comes in the spring of your four hundredth year, and with it a thing the old foxes warned you about: the lamps. Four tails you could fold into a person's shadow. Five will not fold. You light the lamp in your borrowed room one evening and there they are on the paper wall, five of them, as plain as washing on a line.

choices.text: Learn to sit with your back to every lamp

effects.log: A whole year of arranging rooms: the lamp behind, the wall in front, the shadow always on the floor where nobody looks. You get very good at it. It is the first thing about the fifth tail that you learn, and the most useful.

choices.text: Count them out loud, one by one, with pride

effects.log: One for the earth, one for the first face, one for the wine-house, one for the bead, and one for this. Five. The vixen who bore you had two, and hid one even from you. You do not hide them from yourself.

choices.text: Blow the lamp out and live by moonlight

effects.log: A year without lamps. You see in the dark anyway. The neighbours think you are thrifty, then stingy, then strange. The bead likes the moonlight better, and grows a little.

events.text: The sixth tail. The old foxes say six is where hiding stops being a trick and becomes a way of life, and you think of every fox you have heard of who lived sixty years among people and was never once seen. Six tails and nobody saw. You had not understood, until tonight, how hard that was.

choices.text: Go and find Banya, and ask how she did it

effects.log: She is older and thinner and wears the same good jacket. "How?" she says. "Every night. One night at a time. And the dog. Always make friends with the dog first." She pours you barley tea. It is the best advice anyone ever gave you.

choices.text: Practise hiding the sixth tail for a whole season

effects.log: It aches, held in. By autumn you can sit in a lit room for a whole evening with only a person's shadow. By winter you can do it while laughing. That is the hard part: hiding while laughing.

choices.text: Sit on the mound and let all six show to the moon

effects.log: Six tails fanned on the frost. The moon does not care how many you have. The village dogs do, and bark all night. You let them. Some nights are for being seen.

events.text: The seventh tail. At a wine-house a storyteller reads aloud from a popular novel about a country of women ruled by a fox queen with seven tails, and the hero who defeats her with a yellow dog that leaps out of a scrap of hide. The drinkers cheer the dog. You sit very still with your seven tails folded small, and a cup in your hand.

choices.text: Cheer the dog with everyone else

effects.log: You cheer louder than anyone. The storyteller bows to you. Somewhere under your skin seven tails are laughing at the joke, or crying, you cannot tell which.

choices.text: Ask the storyteller what the fox queen wanted

effects.log: The storyteller blinks. Nobody has ever asked. "To be a country," the storyteller says at last, slowly. "To have somewhere to be." The wine-house goes quiet for a moment, and then someone calls for another chapter.

choices.text: Leave before the dog comes into the story

effects.log: You put down your coins and go out into the night before the dog leaps out of the hide. You never hear the end. You know how it ends. It ends with a dog.

events.text: The eighth tail opens on a winter night in a borrowed room, and when you light the lamp your shadow on the paper door has eight tails, eight, fanned like a folding screen. You hold your breath. Nobody in the house stirs. Out in the yard, the dog is standing up very straight, looking at the door, and not making a sound.

choices.text: Put the lamp out, and meet the dog's eyes through the paper

effects.log: In the dark the dog sighs and lies down again. It saw. Only dogs see, now, and salt peddlers. Everyone else in the world sees a person. Eight tails, and the whole human world is blind except for the dogs.

choices.text: Leave the lamp burning, and sit with the eight of them a while

effects.log: You sit with your shadow until the oil runs out, eight tails on the paper door, and the dog watching from the yard the whole time. At dawn the dog comes to the step and lies across it, as if guarding something. You think, perhaps, it is.

choices.text: Go out to the dog in the yard

ok.log: You sit down in the frost a little way from it. After a long time it comes and sniffs your hand and lies down against your knee. A dog that has seen eight tails and decided to keep quiet. You will need a great many like it.

fail.log: It backs away from you with its lip lifted and does not stop barking till dawn. The master comes out twice with a lamp. The second time you are very nearly on the wrong side of it.

events.text: A salt peddler sits down on the step of the house where your borrowed face lives, to rest his A-frame, and looks through the open door at your shadow on the wall for a long time. Then he looks at you. He is very old. "Eight," he says, as if remarking on the weather. "I only ever saw seven, before."

choices.text: Offer him tea

effects.log: He drinks it slowly. "My father carried a stick," he says. "I never did. Too heavy." He finishes the tea, and lifts the A-frame, and goes. At the gate he says, without turning, "Hide the eighth better. The ninth will be worse."

choices.text: Ask what became of the seven-tailed one

effects.log: "Went up a mountain and became something else," he says. "Or died. With foxes it is hard to tell the difference from the road." He goes on his way. You think about that for a year.

events.text: The eighth century is nearly done. You can feel the ninth tail waiting under your skin like a word on the tip of the tongue. The old foxes said it opens one of two ways: on a thousand clean days, or on other people's breath. Tonight, on the mound, the moon seems to be leaning down to look at which.

choices.text: Look the moon in the face

effects.log: You do not look away. Whatever road the ninth tail grows on, it is the road you walked. The moon knows. So do you. There is a kind of rest in that.

choices.text: Count your debts out loud, every breath, every face

effects.log: Every borrowed breath, every pale morning, every face you wore and dropped. You say them to the moon one by one. The list is long, or short. Either way, it is yours, and it is said.

events.text: {npc}, an old ferryman who drinks at your table on wet nights, cannot read or write, and pushes a scrap of paper and a brush across to you. {His} child went to the frontier three years ago and has never sent word. "Write to them," {he} says. "Say what a person says. I never knew how."

choices.text: Write it plainly, in {his} words

effects.log: Eat properly. Keep your feet dry. Come home. You write exactly that, three lines, and {npc} has you read it back four times. The letter goes north with a pedlar. In the spring, an answer comes, and {npc} brings it to you to read before {he} lets anyone else.

choices.text: Write it beautifully, the way a scholar would

effects.log: Four lines of good verse about rivers and waiting. {npc} cannot read a character of it, and is very proud. Later you hear that the child laughed out loud at the letter, and then cried, and kept it.

choices.text: Lend {him} the bead for a night, so {he} can write it in {his} own hand

effects.log: For one night {npc} understands every character in the world. {He} writes the letter slowly, in a shaking hand, and in the morning the bead comes back and the understanding goes. The letter stays. It is the only thing {he} ever wrote.

events.text: {npc} comes to the matchmaker with a problem. {His} child loves the potter's child across the river, and has said so, loudly, to everyone, and the two families have not spoken in thirty years over a boundary stone. "Make it a match," {he} says, "or make it go away. I do not care which. I am too tired to care."

choices.text: Make it a match: move the boundary stone yourself, one night

effects.log: You put the stone back where it was thirty years ago, in the middle, which is where it should have been. In the morning both families claim the other moved it. Then, embarrassed, they claim neither did. The wedding is in the autumn.

choices.text: Bring both families to your house and let them shout

effects.log: A whole evening of shouting over your best rice cakes. At the end of it the two old men are crying on each other's shoulders about a dog that died in their youth. Nobody remembers the stone. The match is made.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the truth: you cannot make love go away

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. "Nor can I," {he} says at last. "I only hoped someone could." {He} goes home and walks across the river, and knocks.

events.text: {npc}, a rich landowner, wants a grave site for {his} father: not just a good one, but the one on the ridge where the qi runs down into the neighbour's valley. "Put my father there," {he} says, "and their luck runs into mine. Everyone knows that is how it works. Name your price."

choices.text: Choose {him} a good site, and not that one

effects.log: A quiet slope with a spring below and a pine above. Good for any family, bad for none. {npc} grumbles, then pays, then prospers, mildly. The neighbour never knows how close it came.

choices.text: Tell {him} the qi on that ridge runs the other way

effects.log: It does not. But {npc} believes you, white-faced, and buys a site on the far side of the county instead, as far from the neighbour's luck as possible. A lie, of a kind. The earth does not mind.

choices.text: Give {him} the ridge, and take the price

effects.log: You stake the grave on the ridge. Within a few years the neighbour's valley has had two floods and a fire, and {npc} has bought half of it cheap. Whether it was the qi or only the man, you will never know. You chose the site anyway.

events.text: {npc} pays for {his} medicine in eggs, every week, six eggs in a straw nest, and stays to talk. Today {he} sits with the eggs on {his} knees and asks the question everyone in the waiting room has been wondering for years: "Why do you never get sick? Not once. Not even a cold."

choices.text: "I eat a great many eggs"

effects.log: {npc} laughs until {he} nearly drops the nest. The waiting room laughs too. Every week after that the eggs come with a joke attached. Nobody asks the question again; it has been answered with something better than an answer.

choices.text: "I do. I only get sick at night, when nobody sees"

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, as if that made sense. In a way it does. The next week {he} brings ginger with the eggs, "for the nights." You keep it on the shelf for years.

choices.text: Ask {him} why {he} wants to know

effects.log: "Because if you got sick," {npc} says, "who would look after us?" It is not a question about you at all. It never was. You promise not to get sick. It is an easy promise.

events.text: {npc} has failed the county examination three times and sits in your study with the Analects open at a page {he} has read a thousand times and cannot hold. "You learn things in a night," {he} says. "Everyone says so. Teach me how. I will do anything." The bead in your mouth stirs. It could teach {him} in a night.

choices.text: Teach {him} the slow way: one passage, a hundred times, every day

effects.log: A whole winter of a hundred readings a day. {npc} hates you for a month and loves you by spring. {He} fails a fourth time by one mark, and passes the fifth, and never knows you could have done it in a night.

choices.text: Lend {him} the bead for a night before the examination

effects.log: On your breath, for one night. {npc} sits the examination with the whole of the classics shining in {his} head, and passes high. The bead comes back in the morning. It nearly did not: {he} had heard the old story too, and you saw {him} think about swallowing.

choices.text: Tell {him} the old story about students and foxes on hill roads

effects.log: {npc} listens with {his} mouth open. "Is that true?" "Every word," you say. {He} looks at you very strangely for the rest of the winter, and studies harder than {he} has ever studied, as if someone might be watching.

events.text: {npc}, an old monk of the temple where you wear a novice's grey, finds you in the lamp hall at midnight, where you are supposed to be trimming wicks, sitting with your back carefully to every lamp. {He} sits down beside you, also with {his} back to the lamps, and asks, "What is your name in this life?"

choices.text: Give {him} the novice's name, and nothing else

effects.log: {npc} nods as if that were an answer, and sits a while, and gets up. "A good name," {he} says. "Keep it as long as you can." In the morning the lamp hall has been rearranged so that every lamp faces the wall.

choices.text: Ask {him} what {his} own name was, before

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "Something else," {he} says. "Everyone here was someone else once. You are not as strange as you think." It is the most comforting thing anyone has said to you in a hundred years.

choices.text: Tell {him} your first name, the sound from the earth under the mound

effects.log: It is not a human sound. {npc} does not flinch. {He} says it back, badly, and bows, and from that night on uses it when you are alone, and the novice's name when you are not.

events.text: A face-reader with a mat and a painted chart sets up by your door on market day. {npc} reads three customers, cheerfully, and then looks up at you in the doorway, and stops in the middle of a sentence, and starts to pack the mat away very quickly.

choices.text: Ask {him} to read your face, and pay double

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time and says: "A long life. Many houses. A great deal of hiding. A road that goes up, if you can stop borrowing." Then {he} gives back the coins and leaves. Every word was true. You find that hard to forgive.

choices.text: Let {him} go, and leave rice cakes on the mat next market day

effects.log: {npc} finds the rice cakes and looks at your door a long time, and comes back, and sets up on the far side of the market, and never reads your face again. You are friends of a kind: two people who know too much about faces.

events.text: {npc}, a soldier home from the frontier, cannot sleep. {He} sits at your table every night until the last lamp and does not drink, only holds the cup. Tonight {he} says, without looking up: "Something walked beside our column in the snow for three nights and led us out. A light. Was it you? People say things about you."

choices.text: "Yes"

effects.log: {npc} puts the cup down and looks at you for a long time, and then nods, and goes home, and sleeps for the first time in a year. It was not you. It was some other fox. But {he} needed it to be someone, and you were here.

choices.text: "No. But I am glad something did"

effects.log: {npc} nods. "So am I," {he} says. That is all. But the next night {he} drinks the cup, and the night after that {he} laughs at something, and by spring {he} is asleep before the lamps are out.

choices.text: Sit with {him} until dawn and say nothing at all

effects.log: All night, one lamp, two people not talking. At dawn {npc} gets up and says thank you as if you had said a great deal. Perhaps you had.

events.text: A child of the lane, {npc}, about seven, sits on your step every afternoon to watch the market. Today the lamp is lit early for the rain, and {npc} looks from {his} own small shadow on the step to yours on the wall, and back, and asks with great interest: "Why does yours have more?"

choices.text: "Because I am older"

effects.log: {npc} considers this and accepts it entirely. "When I am old will I have more?" "If you are very lucky," you say. {He} goes off delighted, and tells everyone, and nobody believes {him}, and that is the safest thing a child can do with a secret.

choices.text: Move the lamp, and say it was only the lamp

effects.log: The shadow shrinks. {npc} frowns at the lamp, then at you, then shrugs. Children forgive lamps easily. You feel worse about lying to a seven-year-old than to any king.

choices.text: Show {him} how to make a fox with {his} hands in the lamplight

effects.log: Two fingers for ears, a thumb for the jaw. The fox on the wall barks and bites. {npc} is enchanted, and spends the rest of the rain making foxes, and never asks about your shadow again. It is, in a way, the truth.

events.text: {npc}, whom you have known since you put on this face, comes to you at night with a confession: {he} took money from the temple box years ago, and has never told anyone, and the old monk who was blamed for it is dying. "You always know what to do," {he} says. "I do not know why I think that. Tell me what to do."

choices.text: "Go to the old monk tonight and say it"

effects.log: {npc} goes, white as rice. In the morning {he} comes back with red eyes and says the old monk laughed, and held {his} hand, and said it had been known for years and only wanted saying. The monk dies at peace a week later.

choices.text: "Pay it back first, quietly, and then go to the old monk"

effects.log: {npc} sells a good jacket and puts the money in the box at dawn, and then goes to the monk. It is the right order. You are good at the order of things; it comes of having so many things to hide.

choices.text: "Keep it. A secret kept is a kindness to everyone"

effects.log: {npc} looks at you, relieved, and keeps it. The old monk dies blamed. You know exactly why you gave that advice, and it was not for {npc}'s sake.

events.text: {npc} has known your borrowed face for many years, and has grown grey in them, and you have not. {He} says so at last, over the evening meal, not accusing, only curious: "What do you eat? Tell me. I will eat it too."

choices.text: Give {him} a recipe: pine nuts, ginseng, and no worry

effects.log: {npc} follows it faithfully for a year and feels wonderful and grows exactly as grey as before. "It is the worry part," {he} says. "I cannot do the worry part." Nobody can. You could not either, until you had a very long time to practise.

choices.text: Age your face a little, with the bead, so {he} stops asking

effects.log: A line at the eye, a grey hair. {npc} notices within the week and is so pleased that you are getting old at last that {he} buys you a walking stick. You use it. It is the least you can do.

choices.text: "I am older than you think, and it is not as good as it looks"

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time and does not ask anything else. But {he} stops envying you, which is a gift, and starts, a little, to pity you, which is another.

events.text: {npc}, a cook of the royal kitchens, catches your sleeve in the kitchen court. {He} has been told to send up a soup for the king tonight by a minister who never sends for soup, and the minister's servant stood over the pot for a long time. "You are a physician," {he} whispers. "Taste it. Tell me I am being a fool."

choices.text: Taste it

effects.log: You taste it, and spit it out at once, and your tongue goes numb to the root. Not a fool. You pour the pot into the drain, and {npc} sends up a different soup, and the next morning a minister is very surprised to see the king at council. (-6 health)

choices.text: Smell it, and tell {him} to spill it "by accident"

effects.log: One sniff. A fox knows that smell from the paddies: the root that kills rats. {npc} drops the pot on the step, wails, is beaten for clumsiness, and saves a king. Nobody ever knows but the two of you.

choices.text: Say it is only soup, and stay out of it

effects.log: It goes up. The king is ill for a month and does not die, and a minister rises. You never find out whether you were right to keep out of it. You were safer. It is not the same.

events.text: A rival at the market, {npc}, sells salted fish three stalls down from yours and has noticed that yours never spoils, not in the worst of summer. {He} stands in front of your stall with {his} arms folded and says loudly, for the whole market: "There is something wrong with this fish. And with whoever sells it."

choices.text: Give {him} a whole barrel of it, free, to see for {him}self

effects.log: A barrel of your fish in {npc}'s stall all summer. It does not spoil. {He} sells it, at a profit, and comes back for another barrel. By autumn {he} is your best customer and never says another word about it.

choices.text: Show {him} your salting trick, honestly

effects.log: Sea salt from the west coast, a little pine smoke, and the barrel kept in the coldest corner of the earth under a grave mound, which you do not mention. {npc} learns the first two parts. {His} fish is better. Never as good.

choices.text: Let {his} fish spoil, all summer, by fox-work

effects.log: Every barrel in {npc}'s stall goes off by noon. {He} moves to another market. Everyone in yours now thinks you can curse fish, which is good for business and terrible for a mask.

events.text: {npc}, a wandering swordsman with a scarred face and very good manners, has drunk at your table for a week and never once asked your age, though everyone else does. On the last night {he} pays, and stands, and says: "I came here to kill a fox. I will tell them I could not find it."

choices.text: Ask {him} why not

effects.log: "Your soup," {npc} says. "And the way you gave the beggar the last of it. I have killed many things that deserved it. I am not hungry enough to kill something that does not." {He} bows, and goes, and you never see {him} again.

choices.text: Thank {him}, and give {him} a lantern for the road

effects.log: A paper lantern, lit. {npc} takes it with a small smile. Halfway down the hill road the lantern's light turns, for one moment, the colour of foxfire, and {he} laughs out loud in the dark.

choices.text: Draw on {him} first, in case it is a trick

ok.log: It was not a trick. {npc} parries once, steps back, and looks at you with great disappointment. "Now I have to tell them I found it," {he} says, and goes. The story is all over the province by spring.

fail.log: {npc} disarms you in one move and puts your own kitchen knife back on the table. "I said I could not find it," {he} says. "Do not make me a liar." (-15 health)

events.text: The first full moon of the year, and the whole village climbs the hill at dusk to greet it: whoever sees it rise first will have luck all year. They have built a moon-house of straw and pine on the summit to burn when it comes up. Your borrowed face is expected. Everyone will be looking at the moon, and the moon at you.

choices.text: Go, and stand with your back to the bonfire

effects.log: The moon comes up red over the far ridge and somebody shouts. The moon-house goes up with a roar. Every shadow on the hilltop leaps away from the fire, yours longest of all. You keep it on the grass behind you, where nobody is looking. Nearly nobody.

choices.text: Go, and be the first to see the moon

effects.log: You see it a breath before anyone, of course; you have been greeting that moon for centuries. "The keeper!" somebody shouts. A year of luck, they say, and everyone wants to stand next to you. That is the trouble with luck.

choices.text: Stay home with a fever that you do not have

effects.log: The village is disappointed. A neighbour brings you nut-cracking nuts, for the teeth, and a bowl of five-grain rice. You eat them alone in the dark, listening to the shouts from the hill, and feel more of a fox than you have in years.

events.text: Chuseok, the harvest moon. The village is out in the lanes till midnight with songpyeon steamed on pine needles and new rice wine. In the square the women link hands for the circle dance under the moon, and they catch your sleeve as you pass and pull you in.

choices.text: Dance, and keep your eyes down

effects.log: Round and round under the moon, faster and faster, singing. Your feet know the step from centuries of watching. Halfway through a dog in a yard starts barking and does not stop. Nobody else notices. You do.

choices.text: Laugh, slip your sleeve free, and go to bow to the moon alone

effects.log: Up the hill to the mound, with songs coming up behind you. You sit in the full moon of the harvest and breathe it in. Down there they are dancing in a ring. Up here you are, too, in a way.

events.text: A wedding in the lane on a full-moon night, and the whole street lit with lanterns, and every household asked. The bride's grandmother, who has eyes like an owl, has seated you at the end of the table in the brightest place, with three lanterns behind you, as an honour.

choices.text: Accept the honour, and hold the shadow in with everything you have

effects.log: All evening, under three lanterns, with your tails pressed flat as pressed flowers. It aches like holding a breath for four hours. The grandmother watches you the whole time with a small, satisfied smile, as if she had set you a test, and you had passed.

choices.text: Trade places with a cousin of the groom, laughing about the light in your eyes

effects.log: The cousin is delighted to be honoured. You are delighted to be in the dark at the far end. The grandmother looks at the swap, and then at you, and raises her cup very slightly. She knows. She approves of good manners in anybody.
